And he brought them to the land of Shinar, to the house of his god, and placed the vessels in the treasury of his god.<sup>3</sup>Then the king commanded Ashpenaz, his chief eunuch, to bring some of the people of Israel, both of the royal family and of the nobility,<sup>4</sup>youths without blemish, of good appearance and skillful in all wisdom, endowed with knowledge, understanding learning, and competent to stand in the king's palace, and to teach them the literature and language of the Chaldeans.<sup>5</sup>The king assigned them a daily portion of the food that the king ate, and of the wine that he drank. They were to be educated for three years, and at the end of that time they were to stand before the king.<sup>6</sup>Among these were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah of the tribe of Judah.<sup>7</sup>And the chief of the eunuchs gave them names: Daniel he called Belteshazzar, Hananiah he called Shadrach, Mishael he called Meshach, and Azariah he called Abednego.<sup>8</sup>But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank. Therefore he asked the chief of the eunuchs to allow him not to defile himself.<sup>9</sup>And God gave Daniel favor and compassion in the sight of the chief of the eunuchs,<sup>10</sup>and the chief of the eunuchs said to Daniel, "I fear my lord the king, who assigned your food and your drink; for why should he see that you were in worse condition than the youths who are of your own age? So you would endanger my head with the king."<sup>11</sup>Then Daniel said to the steward whom the chief of the eunuchs had assigned over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah,<sup>12</sup>"Test your servants for ten days; let us be given vegetables to eat and water to drink.<sup>13</sup>Then let our appearance and the appearance of the youths who eat the king's food be observed by you, and deal with your servants according to what you see."<sup>14</sup>So he listened to them in this matter, and tested them for ten days.<sup>15</sup>At the end of ten days it was seen that they were better in appearance and fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate the king's food.<sup>16</sup>So the steward took away their food and the wine they were to drink, and gave them vegetables.<sup>17</sup>As for these four youths, God gave them learning and skill in all literature and wisdom, and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.<sup>18</sup>At the end of the time, when the king had commanded that they should be brought in, the chief of the eunuchs brought them in before Nebuchadnezzar.<sup>19</sup>And the king spoke with them, and among all of them none was found like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Therefore they stood before the king.<sup>20</sup>And in every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king inquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters that were in all his kingdom.<sup>21</sup>And Daniel was there until the first year of King Cyrus.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the third year of King Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem (v. 1). And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with some of the temple vessels, which are carried to the land of Shinar and placed in the treasury of his god (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the defeat of God's people happens under God's hand, not outside it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with some of the vessels of the house of God. And he brought them to the land of Shinar, to the house of his god, and placed the vessels in the treasury of his god.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it.

The book of Daniel opens with a national catastrophe. The year is 605 BC. Nebuchadnezzar, the young crown prince who would soon become king of Babylon, had just defeated Egypt and was now the master of the whole region. Jerusalem could not resist him. King Jehoiakim submitted, and Babylon began taking what it wanted from Judah (2 Kgs 24:1). This was the first of several blows. Another deportation followed in 597 BC, and in 586 BC the city and the temple were destroyed.

A careful reader may notice that Jeremiah dates Nebuchadnezzar's first year to the fourth year of Jehoiakim (Jer 25:1), not the third. The most likely explanation is that the two writers count differently. In Babylon a king's first part-year on the throne was not counted as year one, while in Judah it usually was. Daniel, writing in Babylon, seems to use Babylon's way of counting. The two dates describe the same events.

And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with some of the vessels of the house of God. And he brought them to the land of Shinar, to the house of his god, and placed the vessels in the treasury of his god.

Here is the first great truth of the book, and it is hidden in three words: the Lord gave. From the ground it looked as though Babylon's gods had beaten Israel's God. The sacred vessels from God's temple now sat as trophies in the temple of a pagan god. Anyone watching would have drawn the obvious conclusion.

Daniel tells us the true story. Nebuchadnezzar did not take Jerusalem. The Lord gave it to him. The prophets had warned for generations that this would happen if Judah would not turn from its idols. Isaiah had told King Hezekiah that all that is in your house... shall be carried to Babylon (Isa 39:6). What looked like God's defeat was actually God's judgment. He was not absent. He was keeping his word.

Notice too the name the land of Shinar. That is the old name for the region where people once built the tower of Babel (Gen 11:2). The captives were taken to the very place that had always stood for human pride raised against God. The whole book will show that God's kingdom meets that pride and brings it down.

This is where every believer must begin when life falls apart. The question is not only "What has happened to me?" but "Who is ruling over what has happened?" The same God who gave Jerusalem into Babylon's hand later gave his own Son into the hands of sinful men. Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23). The darkest day in history was also under God's hand, and it became the day of our salvation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–7 — New Names in a New World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nebuchadnezzar orders the best young men of Judah's royal family and nobility to be trained in the literature and language of the Chaldeans for three years, fed from the king's own table (vv. 3-5). Among them are Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, who are given Babylonian names: Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The world will try to reshape God's people from the inside out: their education, their appetites and their names.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king commanded Ashpenaz, his chief eunuch, to bring some of the people of Israel, both of the royal family and of the nobility, youths without blemish, of good appearance and skillful in all wisdom, endowed with knowledge, understanding learning, and competent to stand in the king's palace, and to teach them the literature and language of the Chaldeans. The king assigned them a daily portion of the food that the king ate, and of the wine that he drank. They were to be educated for three years, and at the end of that time they were to stand before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king commanded Ashpenaz, his chief eunuch, to bring some of the people of Israel, both of the royal family and of the nobility,

Babylon did not only take gold. It took people. The king wanted the best young men of Judah's leading families (royal family is literally "of the seed of the kingdom", as the ESV notes). This too had been foretold. Isaiah warned Hezekiah that some of his descendants shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon (Isa 39:7). Whether Daniel and his friends were literally made eunuchs is uncertain. The word could also be used as a general title for a court official. Either way, they were now the property of a foreign king, cut off from their families and their future in Judah.

youths without blemish, of good appearance and skillful in all wisdom, endowed with knowledge, understanding learning, and competent to stand in the king's palace, and to teach them the literature and language of the Chaldeans.

The plan was clever. Babylon chose young men, probably in their teens, who were healthy, handsome and intelligent. It then gave them the finest education in the ancient world. The Chaldeans were Babylon's learned class. Their literature included science and mathematics, but also astrology, magic and the reading of omens. These young Jews would learn to think like Babylonians, and then serve Babylon for the rest of their lives.

It is not wrong in itself to learn the wisdom of an unbelieving culture. Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22), and he did not become an Egyptian at heart. Daniel and his friends did not refuse the education. They learned it, and learned it very well. The danger was not in knowing Babylon's books. The danger was in being shaped by Babylon's view of the world until they forgot who they were.

The king assigned them a daily portion of the food that the king ate, and of the wine that he drank. They were to be educated for three years, and at the end of that time they were to stand before the king.

The generosity was part of the strategy. To eat from the king's own table was a great honor, and it also made the young men dependent on the king. They would owe him everything: their education, their careers, their daily bread. The goal was to make them grateful, comfortable and loyal.

The world still works this way. It rarely begins by demanding that believers deny Christ. It offers opportunities, comfort and belonging, and slowly shapes what we love. Paul's warning fits Babylon exactly: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Rom 12:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Among these were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah of the tribe of Judah. And the chief of the eunuchs gave them names: Daniel he called Belteshazzar, Hananiah he called Shadrach, Mishael he called Meshach, and Azariah he called Abednego.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among these were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah of the tribe of Judah.

Now the story narrows from a whole group of captives to four young men. Out of all the exiles, these are the ones God will use. The book never lets us forget that they are of the tribe of Judah, the royal tribe of David, from which the promised King would one day come.

And the chief of the eunuchs gave them names: Daniel he called Belteshazzar, Hananiah he called Shadrach, Mishael he called Meshach, and Azariah he called Abednego.

The final step was to change their names. In the ancient world a name was more than a label. It told you who a person belonged to. The four had been given names by believing parents in Judah. Now they were given names chosen by Babylon. Later Nebuchadnezzar himself explains that Daniel's new name was given after the name of my god (4:8). Babylon wanted to erase their past and write a new identity over it.

Interestingly, the young men did not fight the new names. They answered to them. The book even keeps using them. They knew that the name a king gave them could not change who they truly were. Their identity did not depend on what Babylon called them but on whom they belonged to.

That is true for every Christian. The world will name us in many ways, by our job, our failures, our background or what others think of us. But God has given his people a deeper name. Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who are elect exiles (1 Pet 1:1). We are chosen by God and living for now as exiles, and no one can take that name away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank (v. 8). God gives him favor with the chief of the eunuchs (v. 9), who fears for his own head (v. 10). Daniel proposes a ten-day test of vegetables and water (vv. 11-14), and at the end the four look healthier than all the others, so their diet is allowed to continue (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Faithfulness draws a clear line and holds it with courtesy, wisdom and trust in God.

verseByVerse.quote: But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank. Therefore he asked the chief of the eunuchs to allow him not to defile himself. And God gave Daniel favor and compassion in the sight of the chief of the eunuchs, and the chief of the eunuchs said to Daniel, "I fear my lord the king, who assigned your food and your drink; for why should he see that you were in worse condition than the youths who are of your own age? So you would endanger my head with the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank. Therefore he asked the chief of the eunuchs to allow him not to defile himself.

This is the turning point of the chapter. Daniel accepted the education and the new name. But here he drew a line. He resolved, deciding firmly in his heart, that he would not eat the king's food.

Why this, of all things? The text does not tell us exactly, and readers have suggested several reasons. Some of the food would certainly have broken the food laws God gave Israel (Lev 11). Much of Babylon's meat and wine was first offered to its gods, and Israel had been warned never to eat what was sacrificed to idols (Exod 34:15). And eating from the king's table was a sign of belonging to the king and depending on him. It is probably wise to see all three in the background. What is clear is that Daniel did not think this was a lifelong rule against meat and wine. Later in life he tells us that during a special time of mourning no meat or wine entered my mouth (10:3), which suggests that at other times it did. His refusal here was about this table, this king and this moment.

The deeper point is that there must be a place where God's people say, "This far and no further." Daniel could learn Babylon's language without losing his soul. But he knew that if he gave way everywhere, nothing would be left of him. Faithfulness in a hostile culture begins with small, private decisions made before God, long before any public test arrives.

And God gave Daniel favor and compassion in the sight of the chief of the eunuchs,

Once again God is the one who gave. In verse 2 he gave Jehoiakim into Babylon's hand. Now he gives Daniel favor in the heart of a Babylonian official. The same thing happened to Joseph in Egypt: the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison (Gen 39:21). The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will (Prov 21:1).

and the chief of the eunuchs said to Daniel, "I fear my lord the king, who assigned your food and your drink; for why should he see that you were in worse condition than the youths who are of your own age? So you would endanger my head with the king."

The official liked Daniel, but he was afraid, and for good reason. Kings like Nebuchadnezzar executed servants who displeased them. If Daniel looked thin and weak, it would be the official's head that rolled. His answer is not quite a no, but it is not a yes either.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel said to the steward whom the chief of the eunuchs had assigned over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, "Test your servants for ten days; let us be given vegetables to eat and water to drink. Then let our appearance and the appearance of the youths who eat the king's food be observed by you, and deal with your servants according to what you see." So he listened to them in this matter, and tested them for ten days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Daniel said to the steward whom the chief of the eunuchs had assigned over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah,

Watch how Daniel handles the problem. He does not make a scene or denounce the official. He does not try to go over anyone's head. He goes to the steward who actually managed their food, and he offers a wise and respectful solution.

"Test your servants for ten days; let us be given vegetables to eat and water to drink.

Then let our appearance and the appearance of the youths who eat the king's food be observed by you, and deal with your servants according to what you see."

Daniel's plan protects everyone. It is short, only ten days. It is measurable, since anyone can see the result. And it leaves the final decision with the steward: deal with your servants according to what you see. Daniel calls himself and his friends your servants. He is firm about his conviction and gentle in the way he holds it.

This is a model for believers who work under unbelieving authorities. Conviction does not require rudeness. Peter tells Christians to give a reason for their hope with gentleness and respect, having a good conscience (1 Pet 3:15-16). Daniel was not looking for a fight. He was looking for a way to be faithful to God while honoring the people over him as far as he could.

So he listened to them in this matter, and tested them for ten days.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of ten days it was seen that they were better in appearance and fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate the king's food. So the steward took away their food and the wine they were to drink, and gave them vegetables.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of ten days it was seen that they were better in appearance and fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate the king's food.

The result surprised everyone except, perhaps, Daniel. After ten days the four looked healthier than the young men who had eaten the richest food in the empire. In a world where being well fed was a sign of health, fatter in flesh was high praise.

This is not a chapter about diet. Vegetables and water do not normally make people look better in ten days than those who eat well. The point is that God blessed their faithfulness. The Bible is clear that for Christians food itself is no longer the issue: the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17). The lesson is not "eat vegetables", but "trust God when obedience looks costly." Those who honor me I will honor (1 Sam 2:30).

So the steward took away their food and the wine they were to drink, and gave them vegetables.

The test became the rule. What began as a risky request became a settled way of life for the rest of their training.

We should not miss how this points beyond Daniel. Centuries later another young man of the tribe of Judah was hungry in a hostile place, and the enemy offered him bread on terms that would have meant turning from his Father. Jesus refused: It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone' (Luke 4:4). Daniel held his ground at a king's table. Christ held his ground in the wilderness and at the cross, where the stakes were infinitely higher. He never once gave way, and because of that, he is able to help us when we are tempted. We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin (Heb 4:15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gave them learning and skill in all literature and wisdom, and Daniel understanding in visions and dreams (v. 17). Examined by the king, they are found ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his kingdom and enter his service (vv. 18-20). And Daniel was there until the first year of King Cyrus (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: God honors those who honor him, and his faithful servant outlasts the empire that captured him.

verseByVerse.quote: As for these four youths, God gave them learning and skill in all literature and wisdom, and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams. At the end of the time, when the king had commanded that they should be brought in, the chief of the eunuchs brought them in before Nebuchadnezzar. And the king spoke with them, and among all of them none was found like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Therefore they stood before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for these four youths, God gave them learning and skill in all literature and wisdom, and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.

For the third time in the chapter, God gave. Babylon gave these young men their education, but God gave them the ability to master it. They became experts in Babylon's learning, but their wisdom came from the God of Israel.

Daniel also received something extra: understanding in all visions and dreams. This quietly prepares us for the rest of the book, where Daniel will interpret the dreams of kings and receive visions of the future. His gift was not learned from Babylon's books of omens. It was given by God.

At the end of the time, when the king had commanded that they should be brought in, the chief of the eunuchs brought them in before Nebuchadnezzar.

And the king spoke with them, and among all of them none was found like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Therefore they stood before the king.

After three years came the final examination, and the examiner was the king himself. Notice that the narrator now uses their Hebrew names again, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Babylon had renamed them, but in God's story they are still who they were. They stood before the king means they entered his personal service.

verseByVerse.quote: And in every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king inquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters that were in all his kingdom. And Daniel was there until the first year of King Cyrus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king inquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters that were in all his kingdom.

Ten times better is a way of saying far, far better. The best minds of Babylon, the magicians and enchanters who claimed secret knowledge, could not compare with four young exiles who feared the LORD.

Their story echoes Joseph's. Pharaoh's magicians could not interpret his dreams (Gen 41:8), but Joseph could, and Pharaoh said, Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God? (Gen 41:38). In both stories God places his servants at the heart of a pagan empire, and the wisdom of the world is shown to be empty beside the wisdom that comes from God.

That wisdom has a name in the New Testament. Christ is the one in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3), who became to us wisdom from God (1 Cor 1:30). Daniel's wisdom was a gift from God. Christ is God's wisdom in person. And if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him (Jas 1:5).

And Daniel was there until the first year of King Cyrus.

The last verse of the chapter is short, but it carries a great deal of weight. Cyrus the Persian conquered Babylon in 539 BC. That means Daniel lived and served through the entire Babylonian empire, some sixty-six years from his capture. (He was still alive after that; 10:1 records a vision in Cyrus's third year. The point here is that he outlasted Babylon.)

Think of what that means. Nebuchadnezzar looked unstoppable in verse 1. Babylon's gods seemed to have won. But at the end of the chapter the empire is gone, and the young captive is still standing. And the first year of Cyrus was the year the exiles were allowed to go home (Ezra 1:1). Kingdoms rise and fall. God's faithful servant remains. That is the message of the whole book in a single sentence.

For Christians living as exiles in a world that does not share their faith, Daniel 1 is a map. Do not run from Babylon, and do not become Babylon. Serve well, learn well, and work for the good of the place where God has put you (Jer 29:7). But know where the line is, hold it with humility, and trust God with the outcome. The kingdoms of this world will pass. The King we serve will not.

1.title: Faithful in Babylon
1.overview:
In the third year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon besieges Jerusalem, and the Lord gives Jehoiakim into his hand. Some of the vessels of God's house are carried to the land of Shinar and placed in the treasury of Nebuchadnezzar's god (vv. 1-2).

The king orders Ashpenaz, his chief eunuch, to bring young men of Israel's royal family and nobility, without blemish and gifted in wisdom, to be taught the literature and language of the Chaldeans for three years, fed from the king's own food and wine. Among them are Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, who are renamed Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego (vv. 3-7).

Daniel resolves not to defile himself with the king's food and wine. God gives him favor with the chief of the eunuchs, who fears the king. Daniel asks the steward for a ten-day test of vegetables and water; at the end the four look healthier than the others, and their diet is allowed to continue (vv. 8-16).

God gives the four learning and skill in all literature and wisdom, and Daniel understanding in visions and dreams. When the king examines them, none is found like them; they are ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters of his kingdom and enter his service. Daniel remains until the first year of King Cyrus (vv. 17-21).
1.theology:
God rules over history, even over the defeat of his own people; Babylon's victory was God's gift and God's judgment (vv. 1-2; Isa 39:6-7; Acts 2:23).

God's people live as exiles in a world that seeks to reshape their minds, appetites and identity, and they are called not to be conformed to it (vv. 3-7; Rom 12:2; 1 Pet 1:1).

Faithfulness draws clear lines before God and holds them with wisdom, gentleness and respect toward those in authority (vv. 8-14; 1 Pet 3:15-16).

God gives favor, wisdom and blessing to those who honor him (vv. 9, 15-17, 20; Gen 39:21; Prov 21:1; 1 Sam 2:30; Jas 1:5).

Daniel's faithfulness in a hostile place foreshadows Christ, who refused to live by bread alone and was tempted in every way yet without sin, and who is God's wisdom in person (vv. 8, 17; Luke 4:4; Heb 4:15; Col 2:3; 1 Cor 1:30).

God's servants outlast the empires of this world (v. 21; Ezra 1:1).
1.examples:
Temple vessels on display in a pagan treasury.

Young captives given a new name after a foreign god.

A student who masters a secular education without losing his faith.

A polite ten-day test instead of a public protest.

An official who likes Daniel but fears for his own head.

Four exiles found ten times wiser than the empire's experts.

A captive still standing when the empire has fallen.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams; his spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him.<sup>2</sup>Then the king commanded that the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans be summoned to tell the king his dreams. So they came in and stood before the king.<sup>3</sup>And the king said to them, "I had a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know the dream."<sup>4</sup>Then the Chaldeans said to the king in Aramaic, "O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will show the interpretation."<sup>5</sup>The king answered and said to the Chaldeans, "The word from me is firm: if you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you shall be torn limb from limb, and your houses shall be laid in ruins.<sup>6</sup>But if you show the dream and its interpretation, you shall receive from me gifts and rewards and great honor. Therefore show me the dream and its interpretation."<sup>7</sup>They answered a second time and said, "Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will show its interpretation."<sup>8</sup>The king answered and said, "I know with certainty that you are trying to gain time, because you see that the word from me is firm—<sup>9</sup>if you do not make the dream known to me, there is but one sentence for you. You have agreed to speak lying and corrupt words before me till the times change. Therefore tell me the dream, and I shall know that you can show me its interpretation."<sup>10</sup>The Chaldeans answered the king and said, "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand, for no great and powerful king has asked such a thing of any magician or enchanter or Chaldean.<sup>11</sup>The thing that the king asks is difficult, and no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh."<sup>12</sup>Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed.<sup>13</sup>So the decree went out, and the wise men were about to be killed; and they sought Daniel and his companions, to kill them.<sup>14</sup>Then Daniel replied with prudence and discretion to Arioch, the captain of the king's guard, who had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon.<sup>15</sup>He declared to Arioch, the king's captain, "Why is the decree of the king so urgent?" Then Arioch made the matter known to Daniel.<sup>16</sup>And Daniel went in and requested the king to appoint him a time, that he might show the interpretation to the king.<sup>17</sup>Then Daniel went to his house and made the matter known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions,<sup>18</sup>and told them to seek mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his companions might not be destroyed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.<sup>19</sup>Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.<sup>20</sup>Daniel answered and said: "Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, to whom belong wisdom and might.<sup>21</sup>He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding;<sup>22</sup>he reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.<sup>23</sup>To you, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, for you have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we asked of you, for you have made known to us the king's matter."<sup>24</sup>Therefore Daniel went in to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon. He went and said thus to him: "Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon; bring me in before the king, and I will show the king the interpretation."<sup>25</sup>Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste and said thus to him: "I have found among the exiles from Judah a man who will make known to the king the interpretation."<sup>26</sup>The king declared to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, "Are you able to make known to me the dream that I have seen and its interpretation?"<sup>27</sup>Daniel answered the king and said, "No wise men, enchanters, magicians, or astrologers can show to the king the mystery that the king has asked,<sup>28</sup>but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and he has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will be in the latter days. Your dream and the visions of your head as you lay in bed are these:<sup>29</sup>To you, O king, as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be after this, and he who reveals mysteries made known to you what is to be.<sup>30</sup>But as for me, this mystery has been revealed to me, not because of any wisdom that I have more than all the living, but in order that the interpretation may be made known to the king, and that you may know the thoughts of your mind.<sup>31</sup>"You saw, O king, and behold, a great image. This image, mighty and of exceeding brightness, stood before you, and its appearance was frightening.<sup>32</sup>The head of this image was of fine gold, its chest and arms of silver, its middle and thighs of bronze,<sup>33</sup>its legs of iron, its feet partly of iron and partly of clay.<sup>34</sup>As you looked, a stone was cut out by no human hand, and it struck the image on its feet of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces.<sup>35</sup>Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold, all together were broken in pieces, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that not a trace of them could be found. But the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.<sup>36</sup>"This was the dream. Now we will tell the king its interpretation.<sup>37</sup>You, O king, the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, and the might, and the glory,<sup>38</sup>and into whose hand he has given, wherever they dwell, the children of man, the beasts of the field, and the birds of the heavens, making you rule over them all—you are the head of gold.<sup>39</sup>Another kingdom inferior to you shall arise after you, and yet a third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over all the earth.<sup>40</sup>And there shall be a fourth kingdom, strong as iron, because iron breaks to pieces and shatters all things. And like iron that crushes, it shall break and crush all these.<sup>41</sup>And as you saw the feet and toes, partly of potter's clay and partly of iron, it shall be a divided kingdom, but some of the firmness of iron shall be in it, just as you saw iron mixed with the soft clay.<sup>42</sup>And as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong and partly brittle.<sup>43</sup>As you saw the iron mixed with soft clay, so they will mix with one another in marriage, but they will not hold together, just as iron does not mix with clay.<sup>44</sup>And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever,<sup>45</sup>just as you saw that a stone was cut from a mountain by no human hand, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold. A great God has made known to the king what shall be after this. The dream is certain, and its interpretation sure."<sup>46</sup>Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and paid homage to Daniel, and commanded that an offering and incense be offered up to him.<sup>47</sup>The king answered and said to Daniel, "Truly, your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, and a revealer of mysteries, for you have been able to reveal this mystery."<sup>48</sup>Then the king gave Daniel high honors and many great gifts, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief prefect over all the wise men of Babylon.<sup>49</sup>Daniel made a request of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon. But Daniel remained at the king's court.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — A Dream No One Could Tell
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nebuchadnezzar has troubling dreams and summons his wise men (vv. 1-3). They ask to hear the dream, but he demands that they tell him both the dream and its meaning, or die (vv. 4-9). There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand, they protest; only the gods could, whose dwelling is not with flesh (vv. 10-11). The furious king orders all the wise men of Babylon destroyed, and Daniel and his friends are sought for execution (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Human wisdom reaches its limit where only God can speak.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams; his spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him. Then the king commanded that the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans be summoned to tell the king his dreams. So they came in and stood before the king. And the king said to them, "I had a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know the dream."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams; his spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him.

The most powerful man in the world could not sleep. Nebuchadnezzar ruled an empire, commanded armies and had every comfort money could buy. But a dream frightened him, and he could not shake it off.

There is a quiet lesson here. Power does not bring peace. It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (Ps 127:2). And God sometimes troubles the sleep of the proud because he intends to speak to them. The dream that kept Nebuchadnezzar awake was not an accident. It was the first of God's messages to a king who needed to learn who really rules.

A reader may ask how this can be the king's second year when Daniel's training was to last three years (1:5). The simplest answer is the same way of counting we met in 1:1. The part-year when the king came to the throne was not numbered, so the training could run through that part-year, year one and year two, and be finished early in year two. Whatever the exact timing, Daniel is still a young man, newly placed in the king's service.

Then the king commanded that the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans be summoned to tell the king his dreams. So they came in and stood before the king.

Babylon had a whole class of professionals to deal with dreams. The ancient world believed that dreams could carry messages from the gods, and experts kept long written lists of dream signs and their meanings. The king called for all of them.

And the king said to them, "I had a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know the dream."

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Chaldeans said to the king in Aramaic, "O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will show the interpretation." The king answered and said to the Chaldeans, "The word from me is firm: if you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you shall be torn limb from limb, and your houses shall be laid in ruins. But if you show the dream and its interpretation, you shall receive from me gifts and rewards and great honor. Therefore show me the dream and its interpretation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Chaldeans said to the king in Aramaic, "O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will show the interpretation."

Something unusual happens in the Bible at this point. The ESV notes that "from this point to the end of chapter 7" the book is written not in Hebrew but in Aramaic, the common international language of the empire. Broadly speaking, this Aramaic section is about God's rule over the nations, and it is written in the language of the nations. Chapters 8-12 return to Hebrew and focus more closely on the future of God's own people. The language itself signals that the God of Israel is Lord of the whole world.

The wise men's request was perfectly reasonable. Tell us the dream, and we will look it up.

The king answered and said to the Chaldeans, "The word from me is firm: if you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you shall be torn limb from limb, and your houses shall be laid in ruins.

But if you show the dream and its interpretation, you shall receive from me gifts and rewards and great honor. Therefore show me the dream and its interpretation."

The king's demand sounds cruel and unreasonable, and it was. But it was also shrewd. Anyone can invent an interpretation for a dream once they know it. If these men truly had access to the gods, they should be able to tell him the dream itself. Only then could he trust their interpretation. Nebuchadnezzar was testing whether their wisdom was real.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered a second time and said, "Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will show its interpretation." The king answered and said, "I know with certainty that you are trying to gain time, because you see that the word from me is firm— if you do not make the dream known to me, there is but one sentence for you. You have agreed to speak lying and corrupt words before me till the times change. Therefore tell me the dream, and I shall know that you can show me its interpretation." The Chaldeans answered the king and said, "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand, for no great and powerful king has asked such a thing of any magician or enchanter or Chaldean. The thing that the king asks is difficult, and no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answered a second time and said, "Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will show its interpretation."

The king answered and said, "I know with certainty that you are trying to gain time, because you see that the word from me is firm—

if you do not make the dream known to me, there is but one sentence for you. You have agreed to speak lying and corrupt words before me till the times change. Therefore tell me the dream, and I shall know that you can show me its interpretation."

The king suspects what many of their answers really were: lying and corrupt words, invented to please him and to buy time until he forgot or changed his mind. He sees through them. The wise men of the empire are stalling, and everyone in the room knows it.

Notice the phrase till the times change. The wise men hoped that circumstances would shift in their favor if they waited. A few verses later Daniel will praise the God who actually controls such things: He changes times and seasons (v. 21). The magicians hoped time would rescue them. Daniel knew the Lord of time.

The Chaldeans answered the king and said, "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand, for no great and powerful king has asked such a thing of any magician or enchanter or Chaldean.

The thing that the king asks is difficult, and no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh."

Here the wise men say more than they know. They admit two things. First, there is not a man on earth who can do this. Human wisdom has reached its limit. Second, only divine beings could do it, but they are far away, whose dwelling is not with flesh. The gods of Babylon did not live among people or speak to them.

That is the hopeless conclusion of every religion built by human beings: if there is a God, he is far away and silent. The whole Bible answers it. The true God does speak, as this chapter is about to show. And one day he would do far more than send a message. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). The God who was thought to be far from flesh came and took on flesh in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed. So the decree went out, and the wise men were about to be killed; and they sought Daniel and his companions, to kill them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed.

So the decree went out, and the wise men were about to be killed; and they sought Daniel and his companions, to kill them.

The king's rage is terrifying. In a moment of fury he orders the death of his entire staff of advisers. And the order sweeps up Daniel and his friends too, though they had not even been in the room. This is what life under a pagan king was like. The same man who fed them from his table in chapter 1 now wants them dead.

Believers often find themselves caught up in the consequences of decisions made by powerful people who do not know God. Daniel had done nothing wrong. Yet the executioners were on their way. The question the chapter now asks is: what do God's people do when the sword is at the door?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–23 — The God Who Reveals Mysteries
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel speaks with prudence to Arioch, asks the king for time (vv. 14-16), and gathers his friends to seek mercy from the God of heaven (vv. 17-18). The mystery is revealed in a night vision, and Daniel blesses God: he removes kings and sets up kings; he reveals deep and hidden things (vv. 19-23).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's people are in danger, they pray together, and they praise God before they act.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel replied with prudence and discretion to Arioch, the captain of the king's guard, who had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon. He declared to Arioch, the king's captain, "Why is the decree of the king so urgent?" Then Arioch made the matter known to Daniel. And Daniel went in and requested the king to appoint him a time, that he might show the interpretation to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Daniel replied with prudence and discretion to Arioch, the captain of the king's guard, who had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon.

Daniel does not panic. He speaks with prudence and discretion, calmly and wisely, to the very man who has come to kill him. As in chapter 1, he is respectful toward those in authority even when they are carrying out an unjust order.

He declared to Arioch, the king's captain, "Why is the decree of the king so urgent?" Then Arioch made the matter known to Daniel.

And Daniel went in and requested the king to appoint him a time, that he might show the interpretation to the king.

This is remarkable. The wise men had been accused of stalling for time, and the king was furious. Yet Daniel goes in and asks for time, and he receives it. Perhaps his reputation from chapter 1 helped. Certainly God was at work again in the king's heart. But notice that Daniel promises something he does not yet have. He does not know the dream. He is walking forward in faith, confident that God can do what no man on earth can.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel went to his house and made the matter known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions, and told them to seek mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his companions might not be destroyed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Daniel went to his house and made the matter known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions,

and told them to seek mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his companions might not be destroyed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.

Daniel's first move is not a strategy meeting. It is a prayer meeting. He goes home, gathers his three friends and asks them to pray. Note how they pray. They ask for mercy. They do not demand an answer from God as though he owed them one. They come as needy people asking for grace.

And they pray together. Daniel did not carry this burden alone. Even the wisest believer needs the prayers of others. Jesus promised, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven (Matt 18:19). When Peter was in prison, earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church (Acts 12:5). Christian friendship is at its best when friends pray.

They call God the God of heaven. Babylon's astrologers studied the stars in the heavens to read the future. These four young men prayed to the God who made the heavens and rules them.

They ask for help with a mystery, a secret that only God can make known. The New Testament uses the same idea for the gospel itself. The greatest secret of all, hidden for ages, was God's plan to save people from every nation through Christ. Paul speaks of the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed (Rom 16:25-26). The God who revealed the king's dream to Daniel has revealed his Son to us.

Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.

God answered that same night. And before Daniel rushes to the king to save his life, he stops to worship. His first response to answered prayer is praise.

verseByVerse.quote: Daniel answered and said: "Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, to whom belong wisdom and might. He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him. To you, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, for you have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we asked of you, for you have made known to us the king's matter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel answered and said: "Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, to whom belong wisdom and might.

Daniel's prayer is one of the great hymns of the Bible, and it announces the theme of the entire book. God has two things that the kings of Babylon thought were theirs: wisdom, which the wise men claimed, and might, which the king claimed. Both belong to God.

He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding;

This is the heart of it. He removes kings and sets up kings. Nebuchadnezzar thinks he controls history. In fact every ruler holds power only as long as God allows. The rest of the book will prove this again and again. Nebuchadnezzar will be humbled (ch. 4), Belshazzar removed in a single night (ch. 5), and the great empires of the world will rise and fall on God's timetable (chs. 7-8, 11).

For believers this is deep comfort. Elections, wars and changes of power can make us anxious. But no ruler takes office or leaves it without God's permission. Christ is the ruler of kings on earth (Rev 1:5).

he reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.

What was dark to every wise man in Babylon is light to God. Nothing is hidden from him. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God (1 Cor 2:10).

To you, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, for you have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we asked of you, for you have made known to us the king's matter."

Daniel calls him God of my fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. In a foreign land, far from the temple, he is still Israel's God. And notice the pronouns: what we asked of you and made known to us. Daniel gives credit to the shared prayers of his friends. The answer did not come to a lone genius but to a praying fellowship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — Not Because of Any Wisdom in Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel stops the executions and is brought to the king (vv. 24-26). No human wise man can tell the mystery, but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries (vv. 27-28). The dream concerns what is to come, and it has been revealed to Daniel not because of any wisdom that I have more than all the living (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The faithful witness points away from himself to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore Daniel went in to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon. He went and said thus to him: "Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon; bring me in before the king, and I will show the king the interpretation." Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste and said thus to him: "I have found among the exiles from Judah a man who will make known to the king the interpretation." The king declared to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, "Are you able to make known to me the dream that I have seen and its interpretation?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore Daniel went in to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon. He went and said thus to him: "Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon; bring me in before the king, and I will show the king the interpretation."

Daniel's first words are a plea for others: Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon. These were the pagan astrologers and magicians whose religion Daniel rejected. Yet he intercedes for their lives. God's people are to seek the good even of those who do not share their faith (Jer 29:7).

Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste and said thus to him: "I have found among the exiles from Judah a man who will make known to the king the interpretation."

Arioch is quick to take some of the credit: I have found. Courtiers have always been like that. But his words also remind the king of something important. The man who can do what Babylon's experts cannot is one of the exiles from Judah, a member of the conquered people.

The king declared to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, "Are you able to make known to me the dream that I have seen and its interpretation?"

The narrator reminds us that the king knows him as Belteshazzar, the name given in honor of a Babylonian god. But the God who is about to answer the king's question is not the god of that name. It is the God of the exile standing in front of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Daniel answered the king and said, "No wise men, enchanters, magicians, or astrologers can show to the king the mystery that the king has asked, but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and he has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will be in the latter days. Your dream and the visions of your head as you lay in bed are these: To you, O king, as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be after this, and he who reveals mysteries made known to you what is to be. But as for me, this mystery has been revealed to me, not because of any wisdom that I have more than all the living, but in order that the interpretation may be made known to the king, and that you may know the thoughts of your mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel answered the king and said, "No wise men, enchanters, magicians, or astrologers can show to the king the mystery that the king has asked,

but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and he has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will be in the latter days. Your dream and the visions of your head as you lay in bed are these:

The king asked, Are you able? Daniel's answer begins with a no. No human being can do it, including Daniel himself. Then comes the great but: but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.

Here is a young man standing before the most powerful ruler on earth, with his life on the line, and his first concern is to make sure the king knows who deserves the glory. He could easily have taken the credit and secured his career. Instead he preaches.

The dream is about the latter days, the future that God has planned. The New Testament tells us that those days began with the coming of Christ: in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:2).

To you, O king, as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be after this, and he who reveals mysteries made known to you what is to be.

Daniel gently tells the king what he had been thinking about before he fell asleep: the future of his empire and what would come after him. The great king was worried about what would outlast him. God answered that question.

But as for me, this mystery has been revealed to me, not because of any wisdom that I have more than all the living, but in order that the interpretation may be made known to the king, and that you may know the thoughts of your mind.

Daniel refuses to be admired. Not because of any wisdom that I have. Every gift God gives his people is for the sake of others and for the glory of God. What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? (1 Cor 4:7). The best servants of God are like windows. People look through them and see God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–35 — The Image and the Stone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king saw a great, bright, frightening image: a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, middle and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron mixed with clay (vv. 31-33). A stone was cut out by no human hand and struck the feet, and the whole image was broken to pieces and blown away like chaff, But the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth (vv. 34-35).
verseByVerse.theology: All human empires, however glorious, will be swept away by a kingdom God himself establishes.

verseByVerse.quote: "You saw, O king, and behold, a great image. This image, mighty and of exceeding brightness, stood before you, and its appearance was frightening. The head of this image was of fine gold, its chest and arms of silver, its middle and thighs of bronze, its legs of iron, its feet partly of iron and partly of clay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You saw, O king, and behold, a great image. This image, mighty and of exceeding brightness, stood before you, and its appearance was frightening.

Now Daniel tells the dream. The king had seen a gigantic human figure, a statue shining so brightly that it terrified him. It was a picture of human power at its most impressive.

The head of this image was of fine gold, its chest and arms of silver, its middle and thighs of bronze,

its legs of iron, its feet partly of iron and partly of clay.

Notice the pattern. From head to foot the metals become less precious (gold, then silver, bronze and iron) but harder and stronger, until at the very bottom they are mixed with clay. The whole impressive structure stands on feet that cannot hold together. Human empires look magnificent at the top, but they rest on something fragile.

verseByVerse.quote: As you looked, a stone was cut out by no human hand, and it struck the image on its feet of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold, all together were broken in pieces, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that not a trace of them could be found. But the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you looked, a stone was cut out by no human hand, and it struck the image on its feet of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces.

Then comes the shock of the dream. A stone appears. Compared to a statue of gold and silver, a stone is plain and ordinary. But this stone is cut out by no human hand. No quarry worker shaped it. God made it. And it strikes the statue at its weakest point, the feet.

Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold, all together were broken in pieces, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that not a trace of them could be found. But the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

Everything collapses at once, all together, and is blown away like chaff, the light husks that farmers tossed into the wind at harvest so the breeze would carry them off. The Psalms describe the wicked in the same way: like chaff that the wind drives away (Ps 1:4). All the glory of the world's empires ends as dust on the wind, so that not a trace of them could be found.

But the stone grows. It becomes a great mountain and fills the whole earth. The humble thing that God made outlasts everything humans built, and it takes the place they once held.

Jesus applied this picture to himself. Quoting the psalm about the stone that the builders rejected, he warned, Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him (Luke 20:17-18). The stone that smashes the kingdoms of the world is Christ and the kingdom he brings.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–45 — A Kingdom That Shall Never Be Destroyed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nebuchadnezzar, to whom God has given his power, is the head of gold (vv. 36-38). After him will come a lesser kingdom, a third of bronze, and a fourth strong as iron but finally divided and brittle, like iron mixed with clay (vv. 39-43). And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed; it will end all these kingdoms and stand forever (vv. 44-45).
verseByVerse.theology: History moves toward the everlasting kingdom of God, fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "This was the dream. Now we will tell the king its interpretation. You, O king, the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, and the might, and the glory, and into whose hand he has given, wherever they dwell, the children of man, the beasts of the field, and the birds of the heavens, making you rule over them all—you are the head of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"This was the dream. Now we will tell the king its interpretation.

Daniel says we. He may be including the friends who prayed with him, or speaking as God's messenger together with the God who sent him. Either way, he does not present himself as a lone genius.

You, O king, the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, and the might, and the glory,

and into whose hand he has given, wherever they dwell, the children of man, the beasts of the field, and the birds of the heavens, making you rule over them all—you are the head of gold.

Daniel speaks to the king with courtesy and honesty. Nebuchadnezzar is indeed the king of kings, the greatest ruler on earth. But Daniel makes sure he hears where that greatness came from: the God of heaven has given it. Everything Nebuchadnezzar has, his kingdom, power, might and glory, is on loan from God.

Listen to the description of his rule: over the children of man, the beasts of the field, and the birds of the heavens. It sounds like the dominion God gave to Adam at creation, over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth (Gen 1:28). Nebuchadnezzar has been given a kind of Adam's rule over the world. But like Adam he will grasp at more, and in chapter 4 this king who ruled the beasts will be made to live like one. The book is preparing us for a better ruler. In chapter 7 Daniel will see one like a son of man who receives an everlasting dominion (7:13-14). That is Jesus, the true man who rules in the way God intended. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him (Heb 2:8-9).

You are the head of gold. The first kingdom is Babylon, and the text says so plainly. Nebuchadnezzar must have been pleased to hear it. But he was about to learn that the head of gold was only the top of a statue that would be completely destroyed.

Only one King truly deserves the title Daniel uses here. Paul speaks of God as the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords (1 Tim 6:15), and Revelation gives the same title to Christ: the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (Rev 17:14). Nebuchadnezzar's title was borrowed. Christ's is his own.

verseByVerse.quote: Another kingdom inferior to you shall arise after you, and yet a third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over all the earth. And there shall be a fourth kingdom, strong as iron, because iron breaks to pieces and shatters all things. And like iron that crushes, it shall break and crush all these.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another kingdom inferior to you shall arise after you, and yet a third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over all the earth.

And there shall be a fourth kingdom, strong as iron, because iron breaks to pieces and shatters all things. And like iron that crushes, it shall break and crush all these.

Daniel names only the first kingdom. Who are the others? Christians have answered in two main ways, and it is helpful to know both.

The traditional view, held by the early church, the Reformers and most evangelical interpreters today, sees four empires in order: Babylon (gold), then the Medo-Persian empire (silver), which conquered Babylon in 539 BC, then Greece under Alexander the Great and his successors (bronze), and finally Rome (iron), which crushed everything before it. Daniel 8 supports this. There the kings of Media and Persia are pictured together as one animal, followed by the king of Greece (8:20-21). On this view the fourth kingdom is Rome, the empire in which Jesus was born.

Many other scholars read the sequence as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, treating the Medes and Persians as two separate kingdoms. This reading usually goes with the view that the book was written much later, in the second century BC, and that its predictions end with the Greek kings. The traditional view has strong reasons behind it, including the way chapter 8 joins Media and Persia, and it is the view followed in these notes. But both readings agree on the point that matters most: every human empire, however strong, will pass away.

verseByVerse.quote: And as you saw the feet and toes, partly of potter's clay and partly of iron, it shall be a divided kingdom, but some of the firmness of iron shall be in it, just as you saw iron mixed with the soft clay. And as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong and partly brittle. As you saw the iron mixed with soft clay, so they will mix with one another in marriage, but they will not hold together, just as iron does not mix with clay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as you saw the feet and toes, partly of potter's clay and partly of iron, it shall be a divided kingdom, but some of the firmness of iron shall be in it, just as you saw iron mixed with the soft clay.

And as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong and partly brittle.

The fourth kingdom has a strange weakness. It keeps the strength of iron but is mixed with clay, and the two will never truly bond. It will be divided, partly strong and partly brittle. Rome was famous for its military power, but it was also a vast collection of peoples, languages and rival rulers that never truly held together, and in the end it broke apart.

As you saw the iron mixed with soft clay, so they will mix with one another in marriage, but they will not hold together, just as iron does not mix with clay.

The ESV notes that in marriage is literally "by the seed of men". The rulers of this kingdom will try to unite by intermarriage, perhaps royal marriage alliances like those described later in 11:6 and 11:17, or perhaps a wider mixing of peoples. Whatever the exact reference, it will not work. Human power cannot manufacture lasting unity. Only God's kingdom joins people from every tribe and language and people and nation (Rev 5:9) into one.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever, just as you saw that a stone was cut from a mountain by no human hand, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold. A great God has made known to the king what shall be after this. The dream is certain, and its interpretation sure."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever,

This is the climax of the chapter and one of the great promises of the Old Testament. God will set up a kingdom. It will be different from every other in three ways. It shall never be destroyed. It will never be handed over to another people, as Babylon was handed to Persia. And it shall stand forever.

When the angel announced the birth of Jesus, he used the same language: he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:33). And Jesus began his ministry by saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand (Mark 1:15). Jesus was born in the days of those kings, while Rome ruled the world.

Christians agree that the stone is the kingdom of Christ. They differ on when it strikes the image. Many in the Reformed tradition believe the stone began its work at Christ's first coming. His kingdom started small, like a mustard seed (Matt 13:31-32), and it has been growing through the spread of the gospel ever since, until it will fill the earth completely when he returns. Many other Christians, especially premillennialists and dispensationalists, believe the stone strikes at Christ's second coming. They see the ten toes as a final form of the fourth empire, matching the ten horns of chapter 7, which Christ will destroy when he returns to reign. Both readings honor Christ as the King whose kingdom will outlast every other. The Reformed reading, followed here, emphasizes that the kingdom is already here and already growing. Believers have already been brought, as Paul says, to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col 1:13).

just as you saw that a stone was cut from a mountain by no human hand, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold. A great God has made known to the king what shall be after this. The dream is certain, and its interpretation sure."

The words by no human hand are repeated because they matter. God's kingdom is not built by human politics, armies or cleverness. Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zech 4:6). Jesus said, My kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). The church does not advance Christ's kingdom by becoming another Babylon, but by the gospel.

And the whole message ends with certainty: The dream is certain, and its interpretation sure. Christians can face the rise and fall of nations with confidence. Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe (Heb 12:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–49 — God of Gods and Lord of Kings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king falls before Daniel and confesses, Truly, your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, and a revealer of mysteries (vv. 46-47). He makes Daniel ruler over the province of Babylon and chief over its wise men, and at Daniel's request appoints Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego over the province's affairs (vv. 48-49).
verseByVerse.theology: God vindicates his servants and makes even pagan kings acknowledge him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and paid homage to Daniel, and commanded that an offering and incense be offered up to him. The king answered and said to Daniel, "Truly, your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, and a revealer of mysteries, for you have been able to reveal this mystery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and paid homage to Daniel, and commanded that an offering and incense be offered up to him.

What a scene. The king of kings lies face down before a young Jewish captive. He even orders offerings and incense, the kind of honor given to a god.

The text does not tell us how Daniel responded, and we should not guess too much. When the people of Lystra tried to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas, they rushed into the crowd crying, We also are men, of like nature with you (Acts 14:15). Daniel had already made clear to the king that the glory belonged to God alone (vv. 28, 30), and the king's next words show he had heard it.

The king answered and said to Daniel, "Truly, your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, and a revealer of mysteries, for you have been able to reveal this mystery."

Nebuchadnezzar confesses that Daniel's God is God of gods and Lord of kings. It is a real step, but it is not yet true faith. He still thinks of the LORD as the greatest among many gods, not the only God. In the very next chapter he will set up a golden image and demand that everyone worship it. A person can be deeply impressed by God's power without bowing the knee to him. Nebuchadnezzar's journey is not finished, and the book will follow it to the end.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king gave Daniel high honors and many great gifts, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief prefect over all the wise men of Babylon. Daniel made a request of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon. But Daniel remained at the king's court.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king gave Daniel high honors and many great gifts, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief prefect over all the wise men of Babylon.

The young exile who was condemned to death that morning is now ruler of the capital province and head of the wise men he had just saved. God lifts up the humble. Like Joseph before him, Daniel goes from danger to the highest office in a foreign land.

Daniel made a request of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon. But Daniel remained at the king's court.

Daniel does not forget the friends who prayed with him. He uses his new influence to lift them up too. And this sets the stage for chapter 3, where those three friends, now high officials in the province, will face a test of their own.

The chapter began with a king who could not sleep because he feared the future. It ends with the future revealed. Every kingdom of man will fall. One kingdom, set up by God and centered on his King, will fill the earth. Christians need not fear what tomorrow's headlines bring. The stone has already been cut from the mountain, and it will not stop until it fills the whole earth.

2.title: The Stone That Filled the Earth
2.overview:
In the second year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar has troubling dreams. He demands that his magicians, enchanters, sorcerers and Chaldeans tell him both the dream and its interpretation, on pain of death. They protest that no man on earth can do this; only the gods could, whose dwelling is not with flesh. The furious king orders all the wise men of Babylon destroyed, and Daniel and his companions are sought for execution (vv. 1-13).

Daniel speaks wisely to Arioch, the captain of the guard, asks the king for time, and asks his friends to seek mercy from the God of heaven. The mystery is revealed to him in a night vision, and he blesses God, who changes times and seasons, removes and sets up kings, and reveals deep and hidden things (vv. 14-23).

Brought before the king, Daniel declares that no wise man can reveal the mystery, but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and that it has been revealed to him not because of his own wisdom (vv. 24-30).

The king saw a great image with a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, middle and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron and clay. A stone cut out by no human hand struck its feet, and the whole image was broken and blown away like chaff, while the stone became a great mountain that filled the whole earth (vv. 31-35).

Nebuchadnezzar is the head of gold. After him will come an inferior kingdom, a third of bronze, and a fourth strong as iron but divided, like iron mixed with clay. In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed; it will break all these kingdoms and stand forever (vv. 36-45).

The king falls before Daniel and confesses that his God is God of gods and Lord of kings. He makes Daniel ruler over the province of Babylon and chief over its wise men, and at Daniel's request appoints Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego over the province (vv. 46-49).
2.theology:
Human wisdom cannot reach the knowledge of God; the true God reveals what no man on earth can know (vv. 10-11, 27-28; 1 Cor 1:20; 2:10).

The God who was thought to dwell far from flesh has spoken, and in Christ the Word became flesh (v. 11; John 1:14).

God's people meet danger with shared prayer for mercy and answer God's grace with praise (vv. 17-23; Matt 18:19; Acts 12:5).

God rules history: he removes kings and sets up kings, and every earthly power is his gift (vv. 21, 37-38; Rev 1:5; 1 Tim 6:15).

God's faithful servants give the glory to God and not to themselves (vv. 27-30; 1 Cor 4:7).

All human empires will pass away, and God will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, fulfilled in the kingdom of Jesus Christ, the stone the builders rejected (vv. 34-35, 44-45; Luke 1:33; 20:17-18; Mark 1:15; Col 1:13; Heb 12:28).

God's kingdom comes by his power, not by human hands (vv. 34, 45; Zech 4:6; John 18:36).
2.examples:
An emperor who cannot sleep because of a dream.

Experts who can explain any dream as long as they are told it first.

A prayer meeting called because the executioners are coming.

A young man who praises God before he runs to save his life.

"Not because of any wisdom that I have."

A glittering statue standing on feet of clay.

A plain stone that becomes a mountain.

A king on his face before a captive from Judah.
