And the ram had no power to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground and trampled on him. And there was no one who could rescue the ram from his power.<sup>8</sup>Then the goat became exceedingly great, but when he was strong, the great horn was broken, and instead of it there came up four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven.<sup>9</sup>Out of one of them came a little horn, which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the glorious land.<sup>10</sup>It grew great, even to the host of heaven. And some of the host and some of the stars it threw down to the ground and trampled on them.<sup>11</sup>It became great, even as great as the Prince of the host. And the regular burnt offering was taken away from him, and the place of his sanctuary was overthrown.<sup>12</sup>And a host will be given over to it together with the regular burnt offering because of transgression, and it will throw truth to the ground, and it will act and prosper.<sup>13</sup>Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one said to the one who spoke, "For how long is the vision concerning the regular burnt offering, the transgression that makes desolate, and the giving over of the sanctuary and host to be trampled underfoot?"<sup>14</sup>And he said to me, "For 2,300 evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary shall be restored to its rightful state."<sup>15</sup>When I, Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it. And behold, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man.<sup>16</sup>And I heard a man's voice between the banks of the Ulai, and it called, "Gabriel, make this man understand the vision."<sup>17</sup>So he came near where I stood. And when he came, I was frightened and fell on my face. But he said to me, "Understand, O son of man, that the vision is for the time of the end."<sup>18</sup>And when he had spoken to me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground. But he touched me and made me stand up.<sup>19</sup>He said, "Behold, I will make known to you what shall be at the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end.<sup>20</sup>As for the ram that you saw with the two horns, these are the kings of Media and Persia.<sup>21</sup>And the goat is the king of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king.<sup>22</sup>As for the horn that was broken, in place of which four others arose, four kingdoms shall arise from his nation, but not with his power.<sup>23</sup>And at the latter end of their kingdom, when the transgressors have reached their limit, a king of bold face, one who understands riddles, shall arise.<sup>24</sup>His power shall be great— but not by his own power; and he shall cause fearful destruction and shall succeed in what he does, and destroy mighty men and the people who are the saints.<sup>25</sup>By his cunning he shall make deceit prosper under his hand, and in his own mind he shall become great. Without warning he shall destroy many. And he shall even rise up against the Prince of princes, and he shall be broken—but by no human hand.<sup>26</sup>The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been told is true, but seal up the vision, for it refers to many days from now."<sup>27</sup>And I, Daniel, was overcome and lay sick for some days. Then I rose and went about the king's business, but I was appalled by the vision and did not understand it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Vision at the Ulai
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the third year of Belshazzar, Daniel sees himself in Susa by the Ulai canal (vv. 1-2). A ram with two horns charges in every direction until a goat from the west, without touching the ground, with a conspicuous horn, shatters it (vv. 3-7). The goat's great horn is broken and four horns replace it; from one of them a little horn grows toward the glorious land, throws down some of the host of heaven, exalts itself against the Prince of the host and takes away the regular burnt offering (vv. 8-12). A holy one asks For how long? The answer: For 2,300 evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary shall be restored (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Empires rise and fall at God's word, and even the desecration of his sanctuary has a limit he has fixed.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar a vision appeared to me, Daniel, after that which appeared to me at the first. And I saw in the vision; and when I saw, I was in Susa the citadel, which is in the province of Elam. And I saw in the vision, and I was at the Ulai canal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar a vision appeared to me, Daniel, after that which appeared to me at the first.

This vision came two years after the vision of chapter 7, still before the fall of Babylon. And something changes in the book here that most English readers never notice. The ESV notes at 2:4 that the Aramaic section ran to the end of chapter 7. From this verse to the end of the book, Daniel is written in Hebrew again, the language of Israel. The Aramaic chapters dealt with God's rule over the nations. The Hebrew chapters focus more closely on what will happen to God's own people and his sanctuary.

And I saw in the vision; and when I saw, I was in Susa the citadel, which is in the province of Elam. And I saw in the vision, and I was at the Ulai canal.

Daniel was taken in the vision to Susa, some two hundred miles east of Babylon. At the time Susa was not yet an imperial capital. But it would soon become one of the capitals of the Persian empire. Esther lived there, in Susa, the citadel (Esth 1:2), and Nehemiah served the Persian king there (Neh 1:1). God set the scene of the vision in the future center of the next world power.

verseByVerse.quote: I raised my eyes and saw, and behold, a ram standing on the bank of the canal. It had two horns, and both horns were high, but one was higher than the other, and the higher one came up last. I saw the ram charging westward and northward and southward. No beast could stand before him, and there was no one who could rescue from his power. He did as he pleased and became great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I raised my eyes and saw, and behold, a ram standing on the bank of the canal. It had two horns, and both horns were high, but one was higher than the other, and the higher one came up last.

We do not have to guess what the ram means. Gabriel says it plainly: these are the kings of Media and Persia (v. 20). The two horns are the two peoples united in one empire. The Medes were the stronger partner at first, but Persia came up last and grew higher, until under Cyrus it dominated the partnership. This matches the bear raised up on one side in 7:5.

I saw the ram charging westward and northward and southward. No beast could stand before him, and there was no one who could rescue from his power. He did as he pleased and became great.

The Persian empire expanded west toward Asia Minor and Greece, north toward the Caspian region and south toward Egypt. For two centuries it seemed that no one could stop it. He did as he pleased and became great. That is the recurring sin of empires in Daniel: power that answers to no one. But the phrase is also a warning. In this book, those who do as they please are always about to meet the God who does according to his will (4:35).

verseByVerse.quote: As I was considering, behold, a male goat came from the west across the face of the whole earth, without touching the ground. And the goat had a conspicuous horn between his eyes. He came to the ram with the two horns, which I had seen standing on the bank of the canal, and he ran at him in his powerful wrath. I saw him come close to the ram, and he was enraged against him and struck the ram and broke his two horns. And the ram had no power to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground and trampled on him. And there was no one who could rescue the ram from his power. Then the goat became exceedingly great, but when he was strong, the great horn was broken, and instead of it there came up four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I was considering, behold, a male goat came from the west across the face of the whole earth, without touching the ground. And the goat had a conspicuous horn between his eyes.

A goat charges in from the west so fast that its feet do not seem to touch the ground. Gabriel explains: the goat is the king of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king (v. 21). (The ESV notes it may be "the shaggy goat".) History fills in the name. Alexander the Great crossed from Greece into Asia in 334 BC, and within about three years he had destroyed the Persian empire. No army in the ancient world had ever moved so fast.

He came to the ram with the two horns, which I had seen standing on the bank of the canal, and he ran at him in his powerful wrath.

I saw him come close to the ram, and he was enraged against him and struck the ram and broke his two horns. And the ram had no power to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground and trampled on him. And there was no one who could rescue the ram from his power.

The words of verse 4 are turned back on the ram. Once there was no one who could rescue from his power. Now there was no one who could rescue the ram. The empire that trampled others is trampled. God's justice in history often works like that.

Then the goat became exceedingly great, but when he was strong, the great horn was broken, and instead of it there came up four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven.

When he was strong, the great horn was broken. At the very height of his power, in 323 BC, Alexander died suddenly in Babylon, only about thirty-two years old. He had conquered the known world and could not conquer death. His empire was eventually divided among his generals into four main kingdoms, toward the four winds of heaven, just as the leopard of chapter 7 had four heads. The greatest conqueror of the age was broken in a moment, and his kingdom passed to others. Pride goes before destruction (Prov 16:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Out of one of them came a little horn, which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the glorious land. It grew great, even to the host of heaven. And some of the host and some of the stars it threw down to the ground and trampled on them. It became great, even as great as the Prince of the host. And the regular burnt offering was taken away from him, and the place of his sanctuary was overthrown. And a host will be given over to it together with the regular burnt offering because of transgression, and it will throw truth to the ground, and it will act and prosper.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of one of them came a little horn, which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the glorious land.

Now the vision narrows to one ruler. A little horn grows out of one of the four Greek kingdoms. Readers should not confuse this horn with the little horn of chapter 7. That one came from the fourth beast. This one comes from the third kingdom, Greece.

There is wide agreement about who this little horn is: Antiochus IV, a king of the Seleucid dynasty, which ruled Syria and the lands to the east. He reigned from 175 to 164 BC and called himself Epiphanes, meaning "God made manifest". He campaigned toward the south (Egypt), toward the east (Persia) and toward the glorious land, the land of Israel, which Daniel loved.

It grew great, even to the host of heaven. And some of the host and some of the stars it threw down to the ground and trampled on them.

The horn's pride reaches toward heaven itself. The host of heaven and the stars are probably a picture of God's people, who are elsewhere in Daniel compared to stars (12:3), and of the heavenly armies who stand behind them. The ESV notes that the phrase may mean "some of the host". Antiochus attacked the faithful Jews as if he were attacking heaven, and in a sense he was. To persecute God's people is to make war on God.

It became great, even as great as the Prince of the host. And the regular burnt offering was taken away from him, and the place of his sanctuary was overthrown.

The Prince of the host is God himself, the commander of heaven's armies. The horn sets itself up as God's equal. And it strikes at the heart of Israel's worship. The regular burnt offering was the lamb offered every morning and evening in the temple (Exod 29:38-42). In 167 BC Antiochus stopped these sacrifices, set up pagan worship in God's temple and forbade the Jews on pain of death to keep the Sabbath, circumcise their sons or own the Scriptures. The Jewish history book known as 1 Maccabees records these horrors.

And a host will be given over to it together with the regular burnt offering because of transgression, and it will throw truth to the ground, and it will act and prosper.

Two things stand out. First, all this happens because of transgression. The ESV notes it may mean "in an act of rebellion". Either Israel's own sin opened the door to this judgment, or the horn's rebellion is in view. In fact both were true: many Jews of that time were eagerly abandoning God's law for Greek ways. Second, the horn will throw truth to the ground. Tyranny always attacks truth, because God's truth exposes its lies. And for a time it will act and prosper. God's people must be ready for evil to succeed for a season.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one said to the one who spoke, "For how long is the vision concerning the regular burnt offering, the transgression that makes desolate, and the giving over of the sanctuary and host to be trampled underfoot?" And he said to me, "For 2,300 evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary shall be restored to its rightful state."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one said to the one who spoke, "For how long is the vision concerning the regular burnt offering, the transgression that makes desolate, and the giving over of the sanctuary and host to be trampled underfoot?"

Even angels ask the question God's suffering people ask: For how long? It is the cry of the psalms: How long, O God, is the foe to scoff? (Ps 74:10). It is the cry of the martyrs in Revelation: how long before you will judge and avenge our blood (Rev 6:10)?

The phrase the transgression that makes desolate introduces an idea that will return in 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11: an outrage against God so terrible that it leaves his sanctuary desolate. Jesus himself would take up this language when he warned of the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel (Matt 24:15).

And he said to me, "For 2,300 evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary shall be restored to its rightful state."

The answer is a number, and the number means there is a limit. God has counted the days of the desecration. It will not last one day longer than he allows.

What does 2,300 evenings and mornings mean? There are two main readings. Some take it as 2,300 days, a little over six years, perhaps counting from the first attacks on the faithful to the end of Antiochus's persecution. Others note that the temple had an evening and a morning offering each day, so 2,300 offerings would be 1,150 days, a little over three years. That is close to the time between the desecration of the temple in 167 BC and its cleansing and rededication by faithful Jews in December 164 BC. Either way, God set a date, and the sanctuary was restored.

The Jews celebrated that rededication every year afterward with the Feast of Dedication, known today as Hanukkah. The Gospel of John tells us that Jesus was in the temple at that very feast: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple (John 10:22-23). There, while the people remembered the cleansing of the temple, Jesus spoke of himself as the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world (John 10:36). The true temple, the place where God dwells with man, was walking among them. He was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:21).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gabriel is sent to make Daniel understand: the vision is for the time of the end (vv. 15-19). The ram is the kings of Media and Persia; the goat is the king of Greece, and its great horn the first king; four kingdoms will follow (vv. 20-22). Then a king of bold face will arise, destroy the saints and rise up against the Prince of princes, and he shall be broken—but by no human hand (vv. 23-25). The vision is true but for many days ahead, and Daniel is left sick and appalled (vv. 26-27).
verseByVerse.theology: God tells his people in advance what they will suffer, so that when it comes they will know he still rules.

verseByVerse.quote: When I, Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it. And behold, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man. And I heard a man's voice between the banks of the Ulai, and it called, "Gabriel, make this man understand the vision." So he came near where I stood. And when he came, I was frightened and fell on my face. But he said to me, "Understand, O son of man, that the vision is for the time of the end." And when he had spoken to me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground. But he touched me and made me stand up. He said, "Behold, I will make known to you what shall be at the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I, Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it. And behold, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man.

And I heard a man's voice between the banks of the Ulai, and it called, "Gabriel, make this man understand the vision."

This is the first time an angel is named in the Bible. Gabriel is sent to explain the vision. We will meet him again in chapter 9, and then, more than five hundred years later, he will appear to Zechariah and to Mary. I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God (Luke 1:19). The same messenger who explained the rise and fall of empires to Daniel announced the birth of the King whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:26-33).

Who gives Gabriel the order? A man's voice from between the banks of the Ulai. The book does not say who it is, but he has authority to command Gabriel. Many have connected him with the man clothed in linen who stands above the waters of the stream in 12:6-7.

So he came near where I stood. And when he came, I was frightened and fell on my face. But he said to me, "Understand, O son of man, that the vision is for the time of the end."

Gabriel calls Daniel son of man, the same way God addressed Ezekiel (Ezek 2:1). Here it simply means "mortal man", a reminder of how small Daniel is before the messengers of God.

And when he had spoken to me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground. But he touched me and made me stand up.

He said, "Behold, I will make known to you what shall be at the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end.

What is the time of the end? In this chapter the explanation focuses on the end of the indignation, the period of God's anger against his people's sin, which came to its climax under Antiochus. But the vision also looks beyond him. Antiochus is a preview of a greater enemy who will arise at the final end of history. The persecutor of chapter 8 and the horn of chapter 7 share the same marks: pride, blasphemy and war on God's people and worship. What happened under Antiochus is a pattern of what the church must expect before Christ returns.

And notice the word appointed. The end is not random. God has fixed it.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the ram that you saw with the two horns, these are the kings of Media and Persia. And the goat is the king of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king. As for the horn that was broken, in place of which four others arose, four kingdoms shall arise from his nation, but not with his power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the ram that you saw with the two horns, these are the kings of Media and Persia.

And the goat is the king of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king.

As for the horn that was broken, in place of which four others arose, four kingdoms shall arise from his nation, but not with his power.

Few prophecies in the Bible are so specific. Gabriel names the empires: Media and Persia, then Greece. When Daniel received this vision, Persia had not yet even conquered Babylon, and Greece was a collection of small, quarreling cities. Yet the vision describes more than two centuries of history before they happened.

These verses also help us understand chapters 2 and 7. Here Media and Persia are one animal, and Greece comes next. That strongly suggests that the silver kingdom and the bear are Medo-Persia, the bronze kingdom and the leopard are Greece, and the fourth kingdom is the one that came after Greece: Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the latter end of their kingdom, when the transgressors have reached their limit, a king of bold face, one who understands riddles, shall arise. His power shall be great— but not by his own power; and he shall cause fearful destruction and shall succeed in what he does, and destroy mighty men and the people who are the saints. By his cunning he shall make deceit prosper under his hand, and in his own mind he shall become great. Without warning he shall destroy many. And he shall even rise up against the Prince of princes, and he shall be broken—but by no human hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And at the latter end of their kingdom, when the transgressors have reached their limit, a king of bold face, one who understands riddles, shall arise.

When the transgressors have reached their limit. God allows sin to run its course until the measure is full, and then he acts. The king of bold face is shameless and hard. He understands riddles, meaning he is clever at scheming and double-dealing. Antiochus was famous for his cunning.

His power shall be great— but not by his own power; and he shall cause fearful destruction and shall succeed in what he does, and destroy mighty men and the people who are the saints.

But not by his own power. However frightening he becomes, his strength is given to him. He is a tool in a hand larger than his own. He will destroy... the people who are the saints. The faithful will suffer and die. Daniel is not promised that God's people will be spared. He is told that God is still in control.

By his cunning he shall make deceit prosper under his hand, and in his own mind he shall become great. Without warning he shall destroy many. And he shall even rise up against the Prince of princes, and he shall be broken—but by no human hand.

His weapons are cunning and deceit. He attacks without warning. And in his own mind he shall become great, the same inward pride that brought down Nebuchadnezzar. Finally he goes too far and rises against the Prince of princes, God himself.

Then comes his end: he shall be broken—but by no human hand. These are the words used of the stone in 2:34. Antiochus was not killed in battle. He died of a sudden illness while campaigning in the east in 164 BC. God himself removed him.

The Prince of princes has one final answer to every tyrant. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (Rev 17:14). The rulers of the earth once took counsel together against God's Anointed, Jesus, and crucified him. But they did only whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28), and God raised him from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been told is true, but seal up the vision, for it refers to many days from now." And I, Daniel, was overcome and lay sick for some days. Then I rose and went about the king's business, but I was appalled by the vision and did not understand it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been told is true, but seal up the vision, for it refers to many days from now."

Seal up the vision does not mean hide it. It means preserve it safely, like a legal document sealed for the future. The events were many days from now, nearly four hundred years away. When they came, the faithful Jews who suffered under Antiochus would be able to open Daniel and know that God had foreseen every step of their suffering and had set its limit. For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope (Rom 15:4).

And I, Daniel, was overcome and lay sick for some days. Then I rose and went about the king's business, but I was appalled by the vision and did not understand it.

The vision made Daniel physically ill. He had seen the future suffering of his people and the desecration of God's sanctuary, and it crushed him. Prophecy was not entertainment for him.

And yet, when he recovered, I rose and went about the king's business. He went back to work. Knowing the future did not make him quit his job and wait for the end. He served faithfully in the present while trusting God with the future. That is how Christians should live in light of prophecy too.

Daniel admits that he did not understand it. Even the prophet did not grasp everything he saw. Peter says that the prophets searched and inquired carefully about the things they foretold, and that they were serving not themselves but you (1 Pet 1:10, 12). We live on the far side of these events. We can see how they came true, and we can see in them the pattern of the final conflict before Christ returns. Most of all, we know the Prince against whom every little horn rises, and we know that he has already won.

8.title: The Ram and the Goat
8.overview:
In the third year of Belshazzar, Daniel has a vision in which he is at Susa by the Ulai canal. He sees a ram with two high horns, the higher coming up last, charging west, north and south so that no beast can stand before it. Then a goat with a conspicuous horn comes from the west without touching the ground, shatters the ram's horns and tramples it (vv. 1-7).

The goat becomes very great, but at the height of its strength its great horn is broken and four horns come up in its place. From one of them grows a little horn that becomes great toward the south, the east and the glorious land. It throws down some of the host of heaven, makes itself as great as the Prince of the host, takes away the regular burnt offering, overthrows his sanctuary and throws truth to the ground. A holy one asks how long this will last and is told 2,300 evenings and mornings, after which the sanctuary will be restored (vv. 8-14).

Gabriel is sent to explain that the vision is for the time of the end. The ram is the kings of Media and Persia; the goat is the king of Greece and its great horn the first king; four kingdoms will arise from his nation. At the end of their rule a bold-faced, cunning king will arise, whose power is not his own. He will destroy mighty men and the saints, make deceit prosper, magnify himself and rise against the Prince of princes, but he will be broken by no human hand (vv. 15-25).

The vision is true but must be sealed, for it concerns many days ahead. Daniel is overcome and ill for days, then returns to the king's business, appalled and not understanding the vision (vv. 26-27).
8.theology:
God knows and announces the rise and fall of empires long before they happen (vv. 3-8, 20-22; Rom 15:4).

Pride and unchecked power end in ruin; the greatest conquerors are broken at God's word (vv. 4, 7-8, 25; Prov 16:18).

To attack God's people and worship is to make war on God, and God permits such evil only for a fixed and limited time (vv. 10-14, 24; Ps 74:10; Rev 6:10).

The desecrations of history, like Antiochus's, foreshadow the final enemy of God and his people (vv. 17, 19; Matt 24:15).

The restored sanctuary points to Christ, the true temple consecrated by the Father, whose single sacrifice fulfills the regular offerings (vv. 11-14; John 2:19-21; 10:22, 36; Heb 10:11-12).

Every enemy who rises against the Prince of princes is broken by God, and Christ the Lamb conquers (v. 25; Rev 17:14; Acts 4:26-28).

Prophecy is given to steady God's people, and they serve faithfully in the present while trusting God with what they do not understand (v. 27; 1 Pet 1:10-12).
8.examples:
A two-horned ram that no beast can stand against.

A goat moving so fast it seems not to touch the ground.

A world conqueror who dies at thirty-two.

A little horn that tries to trample the stars.

Angels asking, "How long?"

A temple cleansed and a feast still kept.

A tyrant broken by no human hand.

A prophet who is sick for days and then goes back to work.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, by descent a Mede, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans—<sup>2</sup>in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem, namely, seventy years.<sup>3</sup>Then I turned my face to the Lord God, seeking him by prayer and pleas for mercy with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.<sup>4</sup>I prayed to the LORD my God and made confession, saying, "O Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments,<sup>5</sup>we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled, turning aside from your commandments and rules.<sup>6</sup>We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land.<sup>7</sup>To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us open shame, as at this day, to the men of Judah, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, those who are near and those who are far away, in all the lands to which you have driven them, because of the treachery that they have committed against you.<sup>8</sup>To us, O LORD, belongs open shame, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you.<sup>9</sup>To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him<sup>10</sup>and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God by walking in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets.<sup>11</sup>All Israel has transgressed your law and turned aside, refusing to obey your voice. And the curse and oath that are written in the Law of Moses the servant of God have been poured out upon us, because we have sinned against him.<sup>12</sup>He has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us and against our rulers who ruled us, by bringing upon us a great calamity. For under the whole heaven there has not been done anything like what has been done against Jerusalem.<sup>13</sup>As it is written in the Law of Moses, all this calamity has come upon us; yet we have not entreated the favor of the LORD our God, turning from our iniquities and gaining insight by your truth.<sup>14</sup>Therefore the LORD has kept ready the calamity and has brought it upon us, for the LORD our God is righteous in all the works that he has done, and we have not obeyed his voice.<sup>15</sup>And now, O Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day, we have sinned, we have done wickedly.<sup>16</sup>"O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem, your holy hill, because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a byword among all who are around us.<sup>17</sup>Now therefore, O our God, listen to the prayer of your servant and to his pleas for mercy, and for your own sake, O Lord, make your face to shine upon your sanctuary, which is desolate.<sup>18</sup>O my God, incline your ear and hear. Open your eyes and see our desolations, and the city that is called by your name. For we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy.<sup>19</sup>O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. O Lord, pay attention and act. Delay not, for your own sake, O my God, because your city and your people are called by your name."<sup>20</sup>While I was speaking and praying, confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my plea before the LORD my God for the holy hill of my God,<sup>21</sup>while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the first, came to me in swift flight at the time of the evening sacrifice.<sup>22</sup>He made me understand, speaking with me and saying, "O Daniel, I have now come out to give you insight and understanding.<sup>23</sup>At the beginning of your pleas for mercy a word went out, and I have come to tell it to you, for you are greatly loved. Therefore consider the word and understand the vision.<sup>24</sup>"Seventy weeks are decreed about your people and your holy city, to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal both vision and prophet, and to anoint a most holy place.<sup>25</sup>Know therefore and understand that from the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed one, a prince, there shall be seven weeks. And for sixty-two weeks it shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time.<sup>26</sup>And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing. And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end shall come with a flood, and to the end there shall be war. Desolations are decreed.<sup>27</sup>And he shall make a strong covenant with many for one week, and for half of the week he shall put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate, until the decreed end is poured out on the desolator."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the first year of Darius, Daniel perceived in the books the number of years that Jeremiah had said must pass before the end of Jerusalem's desolations: seventy years (vv. 1-2).
verseByVerse.theology: God's promises in Scripture move his people to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, by descent a Mede, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans— in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem, namely, seventy years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, by descent a Mede, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans—

The date is 539 or 538 BC. Babylon has just fallen, as chapter 5 described. Daniel is now an old man, over eighty. He has lived through the whole of Babylon's empire and has seen it collapse in a single night. The new rulers, the Medes and Persians, have taken over. (For the question of who Darius the Mede was, see 5:31.)

in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem, namely, seventy years.

Daniel was reading his Bible. The books were the Scriptures available to him, including the prophecies of Jeremiah, who had been his older contemporary. Jeremiah had said, When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise and bring you back to this place (Jer 29:10). Daniel had been taken captive in 605 BC. Now Babylon had fallen. He did the arithmetic. The seventy years were almost over.

Chronicles explains why the exile lasted seventy years. The land had to make up for the Sabbath years Israel had failed to keep: All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years (2 Chr 36:21). That detail will matter when we come to the seventy "weeks" at the end of the chapter.

Notice what Daniel did when he discovered that God's promise was about to be fulfilled. He did not simply sit back and wait. He prayed. God's sovereign promises never make prayer unnecessary. They make it confident. Jeremiah's own prophecy said so: Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me, and I will hear you (Jer 29:12). The Bible's promises are meant to be turned into prayers.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel seeks God with fasting, sackcloth and ashes (v. 3). He confesses that God keeps covenant and steadfast love, but we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled (vv. 4-6). To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us open shame (vv. 7-10); the curses of the Law of Moses have fallen justly (vv. 11-14). He pleads for God's city and sanctuary, not on the ground of Israel's righteousness but because of your great mercy: O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive (vv. 15-19).
verseByVerse.theology: True prayer confesses sin honestly and pleads only God's mercy and the honor of his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I turned my face to the Lord God, seeking him by prayer and pleas for mercy with fasting and sackcloth and ashes. I prayed to the LORD my God and made confession, saying, "O Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled, turning aside from your commandments and rules. We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I turned my face to the Lord God, seeking him by prayer and pleas for mercy with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.

Daniel's prayer was serious. Fasting meant going without food. Sackcloth was rough, uncomfortable cloth worn in mourning. Ashes were put on the head as a sign of grief and humility. His whole body joined in his prayer, expressing sorrow over sin.

I prayed to the LORD my God and made confession, saying, "O Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments,

Daniel begins with God, not with his own needs. God is great and awesome, and he keeps covenant and steadfast love. Before Daniel speaks of Israel's unfaithfulness, he remembers God's faithfulness. That is where every prayer of confession must begin, or confession turns into despair.

we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled, turning aside from your commandments and rules.

Then comes the confession, and it is thorough. Daniel piles up words for sin: sinned, done wrong, acted wickedly, rebelled, turning aside. He does not make excuses or minimize anything.

And notice the pronoun: we. Daniel is the most faithful man in the book. Enemies searched his life and found no fault (6:4). Yet he does not pray "they have sinned". He stands with his people and confesses their sin as his own. Ezra and Nehemiah later prayed the same way (Ezra 9:6; Neh 1:6). God's law had promised that if his exiled people would confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers, he would remember my covenant (Lev 26:40, 42). Daniel is doing exactly what God asked.

In this Daniel points us to Christ, who went much further. Daniel identified with sinners and confessed sins he shared. Jesus, who had no sin at all, took the sins of his people upon himself. He bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors (Isa 53:12).

We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land.

At the root of Israel's disaster was a refusal to listen. God had spoken again and again through the prophets, to every level of society, from kings to ordinary people, and they would not hear. That is still the root of spiritual ruin: not a lack of God's word, but a refusal to listen to it.

verseByVerse.quote: To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us open shame, as at this day, to the men of Judah, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, those who are near and those who are far away, in all the lands to which you have driven them, because of the treachery that they have committed against you. To us, O LORD, belongs open shame, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you. To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God by walking in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us open shame, as at this day, to the men of Judah, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, those who are near and those who are far away, in all the lands to which you have driven them, because of the treachery that they have committed against you.

Daniel sets two things side by side. To you... belongs righteousness. God was right to send the exile. But to us open shame. Israel had no complaint to make. The scattered people, near and far away, were living proof that God had kept his word.

This is the heart of genuine repentance. It does not say, "God, why did you do this to me?" It says, "God, you are just, and the fault is mine." The tax collector in Jesus' parable prayed only, God, be merciful to me, a sinner! (Luke 18:13), and he went home justified.

To us, O LORD, belongs open shame, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you.

To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him

Here is the turn in the prayer. God has righteousness, and he also has mercy and forgiveness. Israel has only shame, and yet Daniel dares to hope, because mercy belongs to God. Notice the reason he gives: for we have rebelled. He does not say God should forgive because Israel deserves it. He appeals to mercy precisely because they do not deserve it. Mercy is only needed by those who have no case.

and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God by walking in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: All Israel has transgressed your law and turned aside, refusing to obey your voice. And the curse and oath that are written in the Law of Moses the servant of God have been poured out upon us, because we have sinned against him. He has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us and against our rulers who ruled us, by bringing upon us a great calamity. For under the whole heaven there has not been done anything like what has been done against Jerusalem. As it is written in the Law of Moses, all this calamity has come upon us; yet we have not entreated the favor of the LORD our God, turning from our iniquities and gaining insight by your truth. Therefore the LORD has kept ready the calamity and has brought it upon us, for the LORD our God is righteous in all the works that he has done, and we have not obeyed his voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All Israel has transgressed your law and turned aside, refusing to obey your voice. And the curse and oath that are written in the Law of Moses the servant of God have been poured out upon us, because we have sinned against him.

Daniel knew his Bible well. The Law of Moses had set before Israel blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience, including defeat by enemies and exile from the land (Lev 26; Deut 28). Everything that had happened was written in advance. The exile was not a sign that God had lost control or broken his promises. It was proof that he keeps every word, including his warnings.

He has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us and against our rulers who ruled us, by bringing upon us a great calamity. For under the whole heaven there has not been done anything like what has been done against Jerusalem.

(The ESV notes that our rulers who ruled us can be translated "our judges who judged us".) The destruction of Jerusalem was unique because Jerusalem was unique. It was the city God had chosen for his name. The greater the privilege, the greater the fall.

As it is written in the Law of Moses, all this calamity has come upon us; yet we have not entreated the favor of the LORD our God, turning from our iniquities and gaining insight by your truth.

This is one of the saddest sentences in the prayer. Even after the calamity fell, the people still had not turned to God. Suffering alone does not change hearts. People can be crushed by the consequences of sin and still not repent. Only God's grace does that.

Therefore the LORD has kept ready the calamity and has brought it upon us, for the LORD our God is righteous in all the works that he has done, and we have not obeyed his voice.

Again Daniel says that God is righteous (see v. 7), and he will appeal to God's righteous acts in verse 16. He never accuses God. A man torn from his home as a boy insists that God was just in all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day, we have sinned, we have done wickedly. "O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem, your holy hill, because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a byword among all who are around us. Now therefore, O our God, listen to the prayer of your servant and to his pleas for mercy, and for your own sake, O Lord, make your face to shine upon your sanctuary, which is desolate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, O Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day, we have sinned, we have done wickedly.

And now. The prayer turns from confession to request. And Daniel's first argument is history. God once brought his people out of slavery in Egypt with a mighty hand. That great rescue made God's name known among the nations. Daniel is asking God to do it again: a new exodus, this time from Babylon. The God who saved before can save again.

"O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem, your holy hill, because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a byword among all who are around us.

Daniel appeals to God's righteous acts. Here God's righteousness is not only his justice in punishing but also his faithfulness in saving, keeping his covenant promises. And he appeals to God's reputation. Jerusalem has become a byword, a joke among the nations. When God's people are disgraced, God's name is mocked.

Now therefore, O our God, listen to the prayer of your servant and to his pleas for mercy, and for your own sake, O Lord, make your face to shine upon your sanctuary, which is desolate.

Make your face to shine echoes the priestly blessing (Num 6:25). Daniel longs for God's favor to return to his ruined temple. And the ground of his plea is for your own sake. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "for the Lord's sake".) The great hope of every sinner is not what God owes us but what God owes to his own name. He will be true to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: O my God, incline your ear and hear. Open your eyes and see our desolations, and the city that is called by your name. For we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy. O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. O Lord, pay attention and act. Delay not, for your own sake, O my God, because your city and your people are called by your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O my God, incline your ear and hear. Open your eyes and see our desolations, and the city that is called by your name. For we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy.

This verse is the gospel in the Old Testament. We do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy. Daniel, one of the most righteous men who ever lived, brings no righteousness of his own to God. He brings only need, and God's mercy.

That is how every sinner must come to God. Not "accept me because I have tried hard", but "accept me because you are merciful". And the New Testament shows how a righteous God can be merciful to sinners without denying his justice. God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:25-26). In Christ, God's mercy and God's righteousness meet.

O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. O Lord, pay attention and act. Delay not, for your own sake, O my God, because your city and your people are called by your name."

The prayer ends in short, urgent cries. O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. O Lord, pay attention and act. No elegant phrases now. This is the prayer of a man pouring out his heart. And he ends where he began: for your own sake, because the city and people bear God's name. Christians can pray this way too. We bear the name of Christ, and Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Daniel is still praying, at the time of the evening sacrifice, Gabriel comes in swift flight (vv. 20-21). At the beginning of your pleas for mercy a word went out, and I have come to tell it to you, for you are greatly loved (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: God hears the prayers of his people from their first word, and he loves them.

verseByVerse.quote: While I was speaking and praying, confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my plea before the LORD my God for the holy hill of my God, while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the first, came to me in swift flight at the time of the evening sacrifice. He made me understand, speaking with me and saying, "O Daniel, I have now come out to give you insight and understanding. At the beginning of your pleas for mercy a word went out, and I have come to tell it to you, for you are greatly loved. Therefore consider the word and understand the vision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While I was speaking and praying, confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my plea before the LORD my God for the holy hill of my God,

Now Daniel says my sin and the sin of my people. He does not only confess the nation's sins in general. He confesses his own. The holiest man in Babylon knew he was a sinner.

while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the first, came to me in swift flight at the time of the evening sacrifice.

Gabriel, the angel of chapter 8, comes in swift flight. And he arrives at the time of the evening sacrifice. There had been no temple and no evening sacrifice in Jerusalem for nearly fifty years. But Daniel still marked the time of day when the lamb used to be offered. His heart kept the rhythm of worship even in exile. At that hour, God answered.

He made me understand, speaking with me and saying, "O Daniel, I have now come out to give you insight and understanding.

At the beginning of your pleas for mercy a word went out, and I have come to tell it to you, for you are greatly loved. Therefore consider the word and understand the vision.

Two wonderful truths are packed into this verse. First, God answered at the beginning of Daniel's prayer. Before Daniel had finished speaking, the answer was on its way. God is not reluctant to hear his people. Jesus said, your Father knows what you need before you ask him (Matt 6:8).

Second, Gabriel tells Daniel, you are greatly loved. Daniel had just spent the whole prayer confessing sin and shame. And heaven's reply begins by telling him that he is loved. That is how God receives repentant sinners. Every believer in Christ can hear the same word. We are not loved because we deserve it but because God has set his love upon us in his Son.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seventy weeks are decreed about your people and your holy city, to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness (v. 24). From the word to rebuild Jerusalem to an anointed one, a prince, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks (v. 25); then an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing, and the city and sanctuary will be destroyed (v. 26). He shall make a strong covenant with many for one week and put an end to sacrifice, until the decreed end falls on the desolator (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: God has decreed the time of the Messiah, who would be cut off to atone for sin and bring in everlasting righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Seventy weeks are decreed about your people and your holy city, to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal both vision and prophet, and to anoint a most holy place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Seventy weeks are decreed about your people and your holy city, to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal both vision and prophet, and to anoint a most holy place.

Now comes one of the most debated passages in the Bible. We need to go slowly, because it is also one of the most wonderful.

Daniel had been thinking about Jeremiah's seventy years. God answers with seventy weeks. The ESV notes that the word can be translated "sevens". Most interpreters understand these as seventy sevens of years, that is, 490 years. Remember 2 Chronicles 36:21: the seventy years of exile made up for missed Sabbath years, which came every seventh year. Now God announces seventy times seven. The exile was nearly over, but a far greater problem remained. Seventy years in Babylon had not solved Israel's sin. A longer period, fixed by God, would lead to the real solution.

These seventy weeks are decreed. God has set the timetable. And their goal is given in six phrases. The first three deal with sin: to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity. The last three describe what God will bring in: everlasting righteousness, the fulfilment of vision and prophet, and the anointing of a most holy place.

Read those phrases slowly and ask: who could possibly do this? The temple sacrifices never put an end to sin. No return from exile brought in everlasting righteousness. These goals describe the work of Jesus Christ. He came to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Heb 9:26). He entered the holy places by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption (Heb 9:12). He is the fulfilment of all the prophets (Luke 24:44). And the ESV notes that a most holy place could also be "a most holy thing, or one". Many see here the anointing of Christ himself, the true temple, whom God anointed... with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38).

verseByVerse.quote: Know therefore and understand that from the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed one, a prince, there shall be seven weeks. And for sixty-two weeks it shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know therefore and understand that from the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed one, a prince, there shall be seven weeks. And for sixty-two weeks it shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time.

The seventy weeks are divided into three parts: seven weeks, sixty-two weeks and one final week (v. 27). The count begins with the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem. It runs to an anointed one, a prince. That is what the title Messiah means, and "Christ" is the same title in Greek. When Andrew met Jesus he said, We have found the Messiah (which means Christ) (John 1:41). The word was used of kings and priests who were anointed for their office, and above all of the promised King.

(The ESV notes another way of dividing the verse: "there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It shall be built again". On that reading the anointed one comes after sixty-nine weeks.)

Which word to restore and build Jerusalem starts the count? Several decrees were issued by Persian kings. Cyrus allowed the Jews to return and rebuild the temple in 538 BC (Ezra 1:2-3). Artaxerxes sent Ezra to Jerusalem with broad authority in 458 BC (Ezra 7:11-13). And Artaxerxes allowed Nehemiah to rebuild the city walls in 445 or 444 BC (Neh 2:5). Many interpreters have noticed that if you count 483 years (sixty-nine weeks) from Ezra's commission in 458 BC, you arrive at about AD 26 or 27, when Jesus was baptized, anointed by the Spirit and began his public ministry. Others count from Nehemiah's commission, using a 360-day "prophetic year", and arrive at the days of Jesus' ministry and his entry into Jerusalem. The details differ, but both lines of reckoning point to the time of Christ.

Meanwhile, Jerusalem shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time. The books of Ezra and Nehemiah describe exactly that: a rebuilding carried out against opposition, fear and hardship. God's work often goes forward in troubled times.

verseByVerse.quote: And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing. And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end shall come with a flood, and to the end there shall be war. Desolations are decreed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing. And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end shall come with a flood, and to the end there shall be war. Desolations are decreed.

This is the most shocking sentence in the prophecy. After the long wait, the anointed one comes, and then he is cut off. The phrase is used of being killed. He shall have nothing, dying apparently without kingdom, followers or success.

Christians have long seen here the death of Jesus. Isaiah had said of the suffering Servant: who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? (Isa 53:8). The Messiah would not come to be served but to die. When Jesus hung on the cross, abandoned by his disciples, stripped of his clothes and mocked as a failed king, he truly had nothing. But by being cut off, he accomplished the very things verse 24 promised.

Then the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Jerusalem and its temple, rebuilt after the exile, will be destroyed again. Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foretold it: they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation (Luke 19:44). In AD 70, about forty years after the crucifixion, Roman armies under the general Titus did exactly that. The city that rejected its Messiah lost its temple, and it has never been rebuilt. (The ESV notes that Its end can also be read "His end".)

verseByVerse.quote: And he shall make a strong covenant with many for one week, and for half of the week he shall put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate, until the decreed end is poured out on the desolator."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he shall make a strong covenant with many for one week, and for half of the week he shall put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate, until the decreed end is poured out on the desolator."

The final week is the hardest part of the passage, and here Christians differ most. (The ESV notes that each week in this verse can be read "seven".) The key question is: who is he at the start of the verse?

Many in the Reformed tradition, and many Christians before them, believe he is the anointed one of verses 25-26, the Messiah. On this reading Jesus is the one who shall make a strong covenant with many, through his blood. At the Last Supper he said, this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (Matt 26:28). And by his death, partway through that final week, he would put an end to sacrifice and offering. After his once-for-all sacrifice, the temple offerings had no more purpose, and within a generation they ceased forever. The one who makes desolate is then the Roman power that came against Jerusalem, and God's judgment will finally fall on the desolator too. Jesus spoke of the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel and linked it with the coming destruction of Jerusalem (Matt 24:15; Luke 21:20).

Many other Christians, especially dispensationalists, believe he is the prince who is to come from verse 26, a future antichrist. On this reading the first sixty-nine weeks ended with Christ's first coming. Then there is a gap, the present church age, not counted in the prophecy. The seventieth week is still future: a seven-year period at the end of history, when the antichrist will make a treaty with Israel, break it halfway through, stop the temple sacrifices and set up an abomination, before Christ returns to destroy him.

A third group of scholars reads the whole prophecy as ending in the second century BC, with the murder of a Jewish high priest in 171 BC and the desecration of the temple by Antiochus IV (see chapter 8). And some interpreters take the numbers symbolically, as a complete period stretching from the return from exile to the end of all things.

These notes follow the first reading, because it best explains the six great goals of verse 24 and fits the way the New Testament speaks of Christ's covenant and sacrifice. But faithful Christians hold the other views, and we should hold our differences with humility. What all Christians can agree on is the most important thing. God decreed the time of the Messiah's coming. The Messiah would be cut off. And through his death sin would be atoned for and everlasting righteousness brought in.

Think of where this chapter began. Daniel was praying about seventy years and a ruined city. God answered with the promise of a far greater deliverance: not only the return of exiles to Jerusalem, but the coming of the Anointed One who would deal with sin itself. But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son (Gal 4:4). And when Jesus began to preach, his first words were, The time is fulfilled (Mark 1:15).

9.title: Seventy Weeks
9.overview:
In the first year of Darius the Mede, Daniel understands from the books that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah, the desolations of Jerusalem will last seventy years (vv. 1-2).

He seeks God with prayer, fasting, sackcloth and ashes. He confesses that God is great and keeps covenant and steadfast love, but that Israel has sinned, rebelled and refused to listen to the prophets. Righteousness belongs to God and open shame to Israel; mercy and forgiveness belong to God. The curse written in the Law of Moses has been poured out justly, yet the people have not turned from their iniquity (vv. 3-14).

Recalling the exodus, Daniel pleads for God's anger to turn from Jerusalem and for his face to shine on his desolate sanctuary, not because of Israel's righteousness but because of God's great mercy and for his own name's sake: "O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive" (vv. 15-19).

While he is still praying, at the time of the evening sacrifice, Gabriel comes to him in swift flight. At the beginning of his prayer a word went out, for he is greatly loved (vv. 20-23).

Seventy weeks are decreed for Daniel's people and city, to finish transgression, end sin, atone for iniquity, bring in everlasting righteousness, seal vision and prophet and anoint a most holy place. From the word to rebuild Jerusalem to an anointed one, a prince, will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks, and the city will be rebuilt in a troubled time. After the sixty-two weeks an anointed one will be cut off and have nothing, and the people of the prince who is to come will destroy the city and sanctuary. He will make a strong covenant with many for one week, and for half the week put an end to sacrifice and offering, and a desolator will come until the decreed end is poured out on him (vv. 24-27).
9.theology:
God's promises in Scripture do not make prayer unnecessary but move his people to pray with confidence (vv. 1-3; Jer 29:10-13).

True confession honors God's righteousness, owns sin without excuse, identifies with God's people and pleads only God's mercy and the honor of his name (vv. 4-19; Lev 26:40-42; Luke 18:13; Ezra 9:6; Neh 1:6).

God keeps every word he has spoken, both his warnings and his promises (vv. 11-14).

God hears his people from the first word of their prayer and receives repentant sinners as greatly loved (v. 23; Matt 6:8; Heb 4:16).

God decreed the time of the Messiah, who would be cut off to finish transgression, atone for iniquity and bring in everlasting righteousness (vv. 24-26; Isa 53:8, 12; Heb 9:12, 26; Rom 3:25-26; Gal 4:4; Mark 1:15).

Christ made the new covenant with many by his blood and ended the need for sacrifice; the city that rejected him was destroyed (vv. 26-27; Matt 26:28; Luke 19:43-44; 21:20; Matt 24:15).

Christians differ on the timing of the seventieth week and should hold their views with humility, while agreeing on the heart of the prophecy: the Messiah's atoning death (vv. 24-27).
9.examples:
An old man reading Jeremiah and doing the arithmetic.

Sackcloth and ashes in the Persian capital.

A blameless man praying, "We have sinned."

"Not because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy."

A prayer kept at the hour of a sacrifice no longer offered.

An answer sent before the prayer was finished.

"You are greatly loved."

An Anointed One cut off, having nothing, and accomplishing everything.
