verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Man Clothed in Linen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the third year of Cyrus a true word is revealed to Daniel about a great conflict (v. 1). After three weeks of mourning and fasting (vv. 2-3), standing by the Tigris, Daniel sees a man clothed in linen, his face like lightning and his eyes like flaming torches (vv. 4-6). His companions flee in terror; Daniel is left alone, drained of strength, and falls to the ground (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind the events of history stands a glory that overwhelms human strength.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a word was revealed to Daniel, who was named Belteshazzar. And the word was true, and it was a great conflict. And he understood the word and had understanding of the vision. In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks. I ate no delicacies, no meat or wine entered my mouth, nor did I anoint myself at all, for the full three weeks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a word was revealed to Daniel, who was named Belteshazzar. And the word was true, and it was a great conflict. And he understood the word and had understanding of the vision.

Chapters 10, 11 and 12 are one long vision. Chapter 10 sets the scene. Chapter 11 gives the message. Chapter 12 closes it. This is the last vision in the book and the longest.

The date is about 536 BC. Two years earlier Cyrus had allowed the Jews to go home, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled (Ezra 1:1). Many had returned to Jerusalem. Daniel had not. He was now in his mid-eighties, and he was still in Babylon or its region. The prayer of chapter 9 had been answered, but not all of God's people had gone home.

The word was true, and it was a great conflict. (The ESV notes that this could mean "it was about a great conflict".) The vision concerns war: wars between the kingdoms of the earth, and, as this chapter will show, a war in the unseen world behind them.

In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks.

I ate no delicacies, no meat or wine entered my mouth, nor did I anoint myself at all, for the full three weeks.

Daniel does not tell us exactly why he was mourning. But we know what was happening in Jerusalem at the time. The returned exiles had begun to rebuild the temple, and their enemies discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build (Ezra 4:4). The great return was turning into a struggle. It may be that news of this reached Daniel and broke his heart.

His fast was partial. He gave up delicacies, meat, wine and the oil people used to refresh their skin. Notice what this tells us about chapter 1. There, as a young man, Daniel refused the king's food and wine. Here, as an old man, he gives up meat and wine for a special season of mourning. So his lifelong habit was not to avoid them altogether. His refusal in chapter 1 was about that table and that king.

verseByVerse.quote: On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, as I was standing on the bank of the great river (that is, the Tigris) I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist. His body was like beryl, his face like the appearance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like the gleam of burnished bronze, and the sound of his words like the sound of a multitude.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, as I was standing on the bank of the great river (that is, the Tigris)

The date is significant. The first month was the month of Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which ran from the fourteenth to the twenty-first day (Exod 12:18). Daniel's three weeks of fasting covered the very days when Israel celebrated its deliverance from Egypt. Far from Jerusalem, instead of feasting, he mourned and prayed. Three days after the feast ended, the answer came.

I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist.

His body was like beryl, his face like the appearance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like the gleam of burnished bronze, and the sound of his words like the sound of a multitude.

Daniel sees a figure of overwhelming glory. Linen was the clothing of priests and of heavenly beings. The belt of fine gold signals royalty. His body shines like a precious stone. His face flashes like lightning, and his eyes blaze like torches. His arms and legs gleam like polished bronze, and his voice sounds like the roar of a crowd.

Anyone who knows the book of Revelation will recognize this description. John saw the risen Christ with eyes like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters (Rev 1:14-15). Because of this, many Christians believe the man clothed in linen was the Son of God himself, appearing before his birth in Bethlehem. Others believe he was a mighty angel, noting that the one who speaks to Daniel in verses 11-14 had to be helped by Michael against the prince of Persia, which seems unlike the Son of God. Some suggest that the glorious figure of verses 5-6 and the messenger of verses 10-21 are two different beings. The text does not settle the question. But whether we see Christ himself or a messenger reflecting his glory, the lesson is the same: behind the great conflict stands a Lord of unimaginable majesty.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, Daniel, alone saw the vision, for the men who were with me did not see the vision, but a great trembling fell upon them, and they fled to hide themselves. So I was left alone and saw this great vision, and no strength was left in me. My radiant appearance was fearfully changed, and I retained no strength. Then I heard the sound of his words, and as I heard the sound of his words, I fell on my face in deep sleep with my face to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I, Daniel, alone saw the vision, for the men who were with me did not see the vision, but a great trembling fell upon them, and they fled to hide themselves.

Daniel's companions saw nothing, but they felt something, and they ran. Something very similar happened when the risen Jesus met Saul on the road to Damascus: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one (Acts 9:7). God's presence can be real and terrifying even to those who do not see it.

So I was left alone and saw this great vision, and no strength was left in me. My radiant appearance was fearfully changed, and I retained no strength.

Daniel is left alone. His strength drains away. The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "My splendor was changed to ruin". Whatever dignity and health he had as a great official of the empire collapsed in a moment. Before true glory, human glory disappears. Isaiah said the same when he saw the LORD: Woe is me! For I am lost (Isa 6:5).

Then I heard the sound of his words, and as I heard the sound of his words, I fell on my face in deep sleep with my face to the ground.

Daniel collapses face down, overwhelmed into a kind of faint. This is not what people usually expect when they imagine meeting God or his messengers. They imagine comfort and excitement. The Bible shows people falling down. We need to recover a sense of God's holiness. The one we worship is not a friendly idea. He is the glorious Lord of heaven.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–21 — Fear Not, Man Greatly Loved
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A hand touches Daniel: O Daniel, man greatly loved, from the first day that you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words have been heard (vv. 10-12). The messenger was withstood twenty-one days by the prince of the kingdom of Persia until Michael came to help (v. 13), and he has come to explain the latter days (v. 14). Daniel is strengthened again and again (vv. 15-19). The messenger will return to fight the prince of Persia, then the prince of Greece, with only Michael, your prince, beside him (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer is heard at once, even when the answer is delayed by a spiritual conflict God's people cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a hand touched me and set me trembling on my hands and knees. And he said to me, "O Daniel, man greatly loved, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright, for now I have been sent to you." And when he had spoken this word to me, I stood up trembling. Then he said to me, "Fear not, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words have been heard, and I have come because of your words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, a hand touched me and set me trembling on my hands and knees.

And he said to me, "O Daniel, man greatly loved, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright, for now I have been sent to you." And when he had spoken this word to me, I stood up trembling.

Step by step Daniel is raised. A hand touches him and lifts him to his hands and knees. Then a word lifts him to his feet. And the first thing he hears, as in 9:23, is that he is greatly loved. When the disciples fell on their faces at the transfiguration, Jesus came and touched them, saying, "Rise, and have no fear" (Matt 17:7). The God whose glory knocks us down is the God whose love lifts us up.

Then he said to me, "Fear not, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words have been heard, and I have come because of your words.

This is wonderful news for anyone who prays. Daniel's prayer was heard from the first day. God did not wait three weeks to listen. What delayed was the arrival of the answer, not God's attention.

Notice the kind of prayer that was heard. Daniel set your heart to understand, seeking God's truth. And he humbled yourself before your God. God is near to those who seek him humbly. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit (Ps 34:18).

verseByVerse.quote: The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days, but Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, for I was left there with the kings of Persia, and came to make you understand what is to happen to your people in the latter days. For the vision is for days yet to come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days, but Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, for I was left there with the kings of Persia,

Now the curtain is pulled back on something the Bible rarely shows us. Why did the answer take three weeks? Because the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted God's messenger for twenty-one days, exactly the length of Daniel's fast.

This prince cannot be the human king of Persia. No human king could hold back an angel from heaven. He is a spiritual being, an evil power working behind the empire of Persia. Against him comes Michael, one of the chief princes, a great angel. The New Testament calls him the archangel Michael (Jude 9), and Revelation shows Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon (Rev 12:7).

What does this mean for us? Paul says, we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places (Eph 6:12). The conflicts of history are not only political. There are spiritual powers at work behind nations and cultures, opposing God's purposes and God's people.

We should be careful not to go beyond what the Bible says. Scripture gives us very few details about these powers, and it never tells us to try to identify them, map them or speak to them. It tells us to pray, as Daniel did. And it tells us that Christ has already won the decisive victory: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col 2:15).

and came to make you understand what is to happen to your people in the latter days. For the vision is for days yet to come."

The purpose of the visit is to explain the future of Daniel's people in the latter days. That is the message of chapters 11 and 12.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had spoken to me according to these words, I turned my face toward the ground and was mute. And behold, one in the likeness of the children of man touched my lips. Then I opened my mouth and spoke. I said to him who stood before me, "O my lord, by reason of the vision pains have come upon me, and I retain no strength. How can my lord's servant talk with my lord? For now no strength remains in me, and no breath is left in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had spoken to me according to these words, I turned my face toward the ground and was mute.

Once again Daniel is overwhelmed. He cannot speak.

And behold, one in the likeness of the children of man touched my lips. Then I opened my mouth and spoke. I said to him who stood before me, "O my lord, by reason of the vision pains have come upon me, and I retain no strength.

A touch opens his lips, as the seraph touched Isaiah's lips so that he could speak (Isa 6:7). The messenger has the likeness of the children of man. He comes in a form Daniel can bear.

How can my lord's servant talk with my lord? For now no strength remains in me, and no breath is left in me."

Daniel is honest about his weakness: no strength, no breath. He does not pretend to be a spiritual hero. And that is exactly the kind of person God strengthens. My power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Again one having the appearance of a man touched me and strengthened me. And he said, "O man greatly loved, fear not, peace be with you; be strong and of good courage." And as he spoke to me, I was strengthened and said, "Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again one having the appearance of a man touched me and strengthened me.

And he said, "O man greatly loved, fear not, peace be with you; be strong and of good courage." And as he spoke to me, I was strengthened and said, "Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me."

A third touch, and a word of peace. Fear not, peace be with you; be strong and of good courage. These words gathered up the encouragement God had given his servants for centuries. Joshua heard, Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened (Josh 1:9). And the risen Jesus would stand among his frightened disciples and say, Peace be with you (John 20:19).

Notice that Daniel was not strengthened by trying harder. As he spoke to me, I was strengthened. God's word itself gave him strength. That is still how God strengthens his people, through his word. Daniel's response is the right one: Let my lord speak. Once he was strong enough to listen, he was ready to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said, "Do you know why I have come to you? But now I will return to fight against the prince of Persia; and when I go out, behold, the prince of Greece will come. But I will tell you what is inscribed in the book of truth: there is none who contends by my side against these except Michael, your prince.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said, "Do you know why I have come to you? But now I will return to fight against the prince of Persia; and when I go out, behold, the prince of Greece will come.

The messenger must go back to the fight. The spiritual power behind Persia is still resisting. And after Persia, the prince of Greece will come. As the kingdoms of the earth rise and fall, the unseen conflict moves on with them. Chapter 11 will show the earthly side of the same struggle.

But I will tell you what is inscribed in the book of truth: there is none who contends by my side against these except Michael, your prince.

The book of truth is God's own record of what will happen. The future is not uncertain to God. It is already written in his book. The Psalms say, in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me (Ps 139:16).

And Michael is your prince, the angel who has charge of Daniel's people (12:1). God's people are not alone in the conflict. Elisha once prayed for his frightened servant, and the young man saw the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha, and heard, those who are with us are more than those who are with them (2 Kgs 6:16-17).

For the Christian, the comfort is even greater. We are not only protected by angels. We belong to Christ, who has triumphed over every power. Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Nothing in this unseen war, nor angels nor rulers... nor powers, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 8:38-39).

10.title: A Great Conflict
10.overview:
In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a true word is revealed to Daniel concerning a great conflict. Daniel has been mourning for three weeks, eating no delicacies, meat or wine and not anointing himself (vv. 1-3).

On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, by the Tigris, he sees a man clothed in linen with a belt of gold, his body like beryl, his face like lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his limbs like burnished bronze and his voice like a multitude. His companions do not see the vision but flee in trembling. Daniel is left alone without strength and falls on his face in a deep sleep (vv. 4-9).

A hand touches him and sets him on hands and knees, and he is told to stand, for he is greatly loved. His words were heard from the first day he humbled himself, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood the messenger twenty-one days until Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help. The messenger has come to explain what will happen to Daniel's people in the latter days (vv. 10-14).

Daniel is speechless and weak, but one like a man touches his lips and strengthens him, saying, "O man greatly loved, fear not, peace be with you; be strong." The messenger will return to fight the prince of Persia, and then the prince of Greece will come. He will tell Daniel what is written in the book of truth; none contends with him against these except Michael, Israel's prince (vv. 15-21).
10.theology:
Mourning and humble prayer over the condition of God's people are pleasing to God (vv. 2-3, 12; Ps 34:18).

The glory of God and his messengers overwhelms human strength, and it foreshadows the glory of the risen Christ (vv. 5-9; Rev 1:13-17; Isa 6:5; Acts 9:7).

God lifts up those his glory has humbled, speaking love, peace and strength through his word (vv. 10-11, 18-19; Matt 17:6-7; Josh 1:9; John 20:19; 2 Cor 12:9).

Prayer is heard from the first day, even when the answer is delayed (v. 12; Luke 18:1).

Behind the nations are spiritual powers opposed to God, but God's angels contend for his people, and Christ has triumphed over every power (vv. 13, 20-21; Eph 6:12; Col 2:15; Jude 9; Rev 12:7; 2 Kgs 6:16-17).

The future is written in God's book of truth, and nothing can separate his people from his love (v. 21; Ps 139:16; 1 John 4:4; Rom 8:38-39).
10.examples:
An old man fasting through the Passover season.

A figure with a face like lightning on the bank of the Tigris.

Companions who see nothing and run anyway.

Three touches that lift a fallen man to his feet.

A prayer heard on day one and answered on day twenty-four.

A spiritual prince standing behind an earthly empire.

"Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me."

11.text: <sup>1</sup>"And as for me, in the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him.<sup>2</sup>"And now I will show you the truth. Behold, three more kings shall arise in Persia, and a fourth shall be far richer than all of them. And when he has become strong through his riches, he shall stir up all against the kingdom of Greece.<sup>3</sup>Then a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion and do as he wills.<sup>4</sup>And as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven, but not to his posterity, nor according to the authority with which he ruled, for his kingdom shall be plucked up and go to others besides these.<sup>5</sup>"Then the king of the south shall be strong, but one of his princes shall be stronger than he and shall rule, and his authority shall be a great authority.<sup>6</sup>After some years they shall make an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement. But she shall not retain the strength of her arm, and he and his arm shall not endure, but she shall be given up, and her attendants, he who fathered her, and he who supported her in those times.<sup>7</sup>"And from a branch from her roots one shall arise in his place. He shall come against the army and enter the fortress of the king of the north, and he shall deal with them and shall prevail.<sup>8</sup>He shall also carry off to Egypt their gods with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold, and for some years he shall refrain from attacking the king of the north.<sup>9</sup>Then the latter shall come into the realm of the king of the south but shall return to his own land.<sup>10</sup>"His sons shall wage war and assemble a multitude of great forces, which shall keep coming and overflow and pass through, and again shall carry the war as far as his fortress.<sup>11</sup>Then the king of the south, moved with rage, shall come out and fight against the king of the north. And he shall raise a great multitude, but it shall be given into his hand.<sup>12</sup>And when the multitude is taken away, his heart shall be exalted, and he shall cast down tens of thousands, but he shall not prevail.<sup>13</sup>For the king of the north shall again raise a multitude, greater than the first. verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The messenger reveals the truth: three more kings will rise in Persia, and a fourth, far richer, will stir up all against Greece (vv. 1-2). Then a mighty king shall arise, but his kingdom will be broken and divided toward the four winds, not to his descendants (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: God knows the course of empires before a single king is born.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for me, in the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him. "And now I will show you the truth. Behold, three more kings shall arise in Persia, and a fourth shall be far richer than all of them. And when he has become strong through his riches, he shall stir up all against the kingdom of Greece.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And as for me, in the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him.

The messenger of chapter 10 is still speaking. He reminds Daniel that he has been active in the unseen conflict for some time. Since 10:21 has just mentioned Michael, him is probably Michael, whom the messenger supported, though some take it to mean King Darius.

Before we read this chapter, it helps to know what kind of chapter it is. It is one of the most detailed prophecies of history in the Bible. It describes, in advance, nearly four hundred years of wars, marriages, betrayals and invasions. The names of the kings are not given, but the events match the history of the period so closely that readers have always been able to follow them. We do not need to memorize the details. The point is not that every Christian must learn the history of the Greek kingdoms. The point is that God knew all of it before it happened, and that his people can trust him when the kings of the earth rage.

"And now I will show you the truth. Behold, three more kings shall arise in Persia, and a fourth shall be far richer than all of them. And when he has become strong through his riches, he shall stir up all against the kingdom of Greece.

After Cyrus, three more Persian kings followed, and then a fourth who was enormously wealthy. This fits Xerxes I, who ruled from 486 to 465 BC and led a massive invasion of Greece in 480 BC. He is the King Ahasuerus of the book of Esther, who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces (Esth 1:1). His invasion failed, and the conflict between Persia and Greece set the stage for what came next.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion and do as he wills. And as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven, but not to his posterity, nor according to the authority with which he ruled, for his kingdom shall be plucked up and go to others besides these.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion and do as he wills.

This is Alexander the Great, the goat's great horn from chapter 8. More than a century after Xerxes attacked Greece, a Greek king overthrew Persia. He ruled a vast empire and could do as he wills.

And as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven, but not to his posterity, nor according to the authority with which he ruled, for his kingdom shall be plucked up and go to others besides these.

As soon as he has arisen, he was gone. Alexander died young in 323 BC. His empire did not pass to his children, not to his posterity. His half-brother and his young son were both murdered within about fourteen years. His generals divided his lands among themselves, toward the four winds of heaven. The greatest empire the world had seen was broken up almost at once. Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand (Prov 19:21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–20 — Kings of the North and the South
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king of the south and the king of the north make alliances by marriage and break them (vv. 5-6), invade each other's lands and carry off plunder (vv. 7-9), and raise vast armies against one another (vv. 10-13). The king of the north prevails, stands in the glorious land, with destruction in his hand (vv. 14-16), tries a marriage alliance that fails (v. 17), is stopped by a commander from the coastlands and falls (vv. 18-19). His successor sends an exactor of tribute and is soon broken (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The plans of kings rise and collapse, and God's people live in the land between them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the king of the south shall be strong, but one of his princes shall be stronger than he and shall rule, and his authority shall be a great authority. After some years they shall make an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement. But she shall not retain the strength of her arm, and he and his arm shall not endure, but she shall be given up, and her attendants, he who fathered her, and he who supported her in those times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then the king of the south shall be strong, but one of his princes shall be stronger than he and shall rule, and his authority shall be a great authority.

Now the prophecy focuses on two of the kingdoms that came out of Alexander's empire, because they fought over the land of Israel, which lay between them. The king of the south means the Greek kings who ruled Egypt, the Ptolemies. The king of the north means the Greek kings who ruled Syria and the lands to the east, the Seleucids. For about 150 years, Judea was the prize and the battlefield in their wars.

The first king of the south was Ptolemy I. One of his princes was Seleucus I, who had served as a commander under Ptolemy for a time and then built a far larger kingdom in the north.

After some years they shall make an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement. But she shall not retain the strength of her arm, and he and his arm shall not endure, but she shall be given up, and her attendants, he who fathered her, and he who supported her in those times.

About 252 BC the two kingdoms tried to make peace by marriage. The Egyptian princess Berenice was married to the northern king Antiochus II, who divorced his first wife to marry her. It ended in disaster. Within a few years Antiochus died, and Berenice, her young son and her attendants were murdered. Her father, the king of Egypt, had also died. Human peace treaties, sealed with marriages and promises, shall not endure.

verseByVerse.quote: "And from a branch from her roots one shall arise in his place. He shall come against the army and enter the fortress of the king of the north, and he shall deal with them and shall prevail. He shall also carry off to Egypt their gods with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold, and for some years he shall refrain from attacking the king of the north. Then the latter shall come into the realm of the king of the south but shall return to his own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And from a branch from her roots one shall arise in his place. He shall come against the army and enter the fortress of the king of the north, and he shall deal with them and shall prevail.

Berenice's brother, Ptolemy III, came to the throne of Egypt, a branch from her roots. He invaded the northern kingdom to avenge his sister and won a great victory.

He shall also carry off to Egypt their gods with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold, and for some years he shall refrain from attacking the king of the north.

He returned to Egypt with enormous plunder, including images of gods. Notice again how little the gods of the nations can do. They are carried off in wagons by whoever wins the latest war.

Then the latter shall come into the realm of the king of the south but shall return to his own land.

The northern king, Seleucus II, later tried to strike back at Egypt but failed and went home.

verseByVerse.quote: "His sons shall wage war and assemble a multitude of great forces, which shall keep coming and overflow and pass through, and again shall carry the war as far as his fortress. Then the king of the south, moved with rage, shall come out and fight against the king of the north. And he shall raise a great multitude, but it shall be given into his hand. And when the multitude is taken away, his heart shall be exalted, and he shall cast down tens of thousands, but he shall not prevail. For the king of the north shall again raise a multitude, greater than the first. And after some years he shall come on with a great army and abundant supplies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"His sons shall wage war and assemble a multitude of great forces, which shall keep coming and overflow and pass through, and again shall carry the war as far as his fortress.

The sons of the northern king, Seleucus III and then Antiochus III, known as Antiochus the Great, raised huge armies and pushed south toward Egypt's frontier fortress.

Then the king of the south, moved with rage, shall come out and fight against the king of the north. And he shall raise a great multitude, but it shall be given into his hand.

And when the multitude is taken away, his heart shall be exalted, and he shall cast down tens of thousands, but he shall not prevail.

In 217 BC, at the battle of Raphia near Gaza, the Egyptian king Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III and killed thousands of his soldiers. But his heart was exalted. Proud of his victory, he did not follow it up, and he shall not prevail. The win did not last.

For the king of the north shall again raise a multitude, greater than the first. And after some years he shall come on with a great army and abundant supplies.

Antiochus III did not accept defeat. He spent the next years campaigning in the east, rebuilding his power, and when the Egyptian king died and left a young child on the throne, he came back with a larger army than before. Human ambition is persistent. It loses a battle and returns, stronger and hungrier. That is one reason God's people should never place their hope in the defeat of one tyrant. Another will rise. Our hope is in the kingdom that is not passed from hand to hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "In those times many shall rise against the king of the south, and the violent among your own people shall lift themselves up in order to fulfill the vision, but they shall fail. Then the king of the north shall come and throw up siegeworks and take a well-fortified city. And the forces of the south shall not stand, or even his best troops, for there shall be no strength to stand. But he who comes against him shall do as he wills, and none shall stand before him. And he shall stand in the glorious land, with destruction in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In those times many shall rise against the king of the south, and the violent among your own people shall lift themselves up in order to fulfill the vision, but they shall fail.

Egypt faced enemies on every side. And some of Daniel's own people, the violent among your own people, joined in, perhaps hoping to use the wars to win independence for Judea, as if they could make the prophecies come true by force. But they shall fail. God's purposes are never advanced by human violence.

Then the king of the north shall come and throw up siegeworks and take a well-fortified city. And the forces of the south shall not stand, or even his best troops, for there shall be no strength to stand.

Around 200 BC Antiochus III defeated the Egyptians at Panium in the far north of Israel and then besieged their army in the fortified coastal city of Sidon until it surrendered.

But he who comes against him shall do as he wills, and none shall stand before him. And he shall stand in the glorious land, with destruction in his hand.

As a result, the glorious land, Judea, passed from Egyptian control to the northern kingdom. Daniel's people now lived under a new master, and the stage was set for the terrible persecution to come.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall set his face to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and he shall bring terms of an agreement and perform them. He shall give him the daughter of women to destroy the kingdom, but it shall not stand or be to his advantage. Afterward he shall turn his face to the coastlands and shall capture many of them, but a commander shall put an end to his insolence. Indeed, he shall turn his insolence back upon him. Then he shall turn his face back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he shall stumble and fall, and shall not be found.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He shall set his face to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and he shall bring terms of an agreement and perform them. He shall give him the daughter of women to destroy the kingdom, but it shall not stand or be to his advantage.

Antiochus III tried to control Egypt through a marriage. He gave his daughter Cleopatra to the young Egyptian king Ptolemy V, hoping she would work for her father's interests. Instead she took her husband's side. The scheme shall not stand or be to his advantage. Once again a political marriage failed to deliver what it promised.

Afterward he shall turn his face to the coastlands and shall capture many of them, but a commander shall put an end to his insolence. Indeed, he shall turn his insolence back upon him.

Antiochus then pushed west into Asia Minor and Greece. There he met a new power: Rome. In 190 BC a Roman army under the commander Lucius Scipio crushed him at Magnesia and forced a humiliating treaty on him. (The ESV notes that the meaning of part of this verse is uncertain, but the general sense is clear.) Here Rome enters the story of this chapter, the power that on the traditional reading became the iron kingdom of chapters 2 and 7.

Then he shall turn his face back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he shall stumble and fall, and shall not be found.

Weighed down by the fine Rome demanded, Antiochus went looking for money. In 187 BC he was killed while trying to plunder a temple in the east. The man once called "the Great" shall stumble and fall, and shall not be found.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then shall arise in his place one who shall send an exactor of tribute for the glory of the kingdom. But within a few days he shall be broken, neither in anger nor in battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then shall arise in his place one who shall send an exactor of tribute for the glory of the kingdom. But within a few days he shall be broken, neither in anger nor in battle.

His son, Seleucus IV, needed money to pay Rome. He sent an official to collect taxes, and according to Jewish tradition this official even tried to seize the treasure of the temple in Jerusalem. Seleucus was later murdered by a plot, neither in anger nor in battle. The kings of the north keep grasping, and they keep falling.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A contemptible person to whom royal majesty has not been given seizes the kingdom by flatteries (v. 21). He sweeps away armies and the prince of the covenant, deals deceitfully and wars against the south (vv. 22-27), and his heart is set against the holy covenant (v. 28). Forced back by ships of Kittim, he turns in rage on the covenant people (vv. 29-30), profanes the temple and sets up the abomination that makes desolate (v. 31). But the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action; the wise will teach many and suffer, and some will stumble so that they may be refined (vv. 32-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Persecution will come, but those who know God stand firm, and their suffering refines them.

verseByVerse.quote: In his place shall arise a contemptible person to whom royal majesty has not been given. He shall come in without warning and obtain the kingdom by flatteries. Armies shall be utterly swept away before him and broken, even the prince of the covenant. And from the time that an alliance is made with him he shall act deceitfully, and he shall become strong with a small people. Without warning he shall come into the richest parts of the province, and he shall do what neither his fathers nor his fathers' fathers have done, scattering among them plunder, spoil, and goods. He shall devise plans against strongholds, but only for a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his place shall arise a contemptible person to whom royal majesty has not been given. He shall come in without warning and obtain the kingdom by flatteries.

Now the prophecy slows down, because it reaches the man who matters most for Daniel's people: Antiochus IV, the little horn of chapter 8. He was contemptible, and the throne was not rightfully his. The rightful heir was his nephew, who was a hostage in Rome. Antiochus seized power through scheming and flattery.

The Bible's verdict is striking. This king called himself Epiphanes, "God made manifest". His coins called him divine. God calls him contemptible. The way God sees the powerful is often the exact opposite of the way they see themselves.

Armies shall be utterly swept away before him and broken, even the prince of the covenant.

The prince of the covenant may refer to the faithful high priest Onias III, whom Antiochus removed from office soon after he came to power, and who was later murdered. The man who held the highest office in God's covenant people was swept aside by a pagan king.

And from the time that an alliance is made with him he shall act deceitfully, and he shall become strong with a small people.

Antiochus made agreements and then broke them. And he rose to power with only a small people, a small band of supporters. Tyrants rarely begin with the backing of the many. A determined, deceitful few can seize a great deal of power when others are careless.

Without warning he shall come into the richest parts of the province, and he shall do what neither his fathers nor his fathers' fathers have done, scattering among them plunder, spoil, and goods. He shall devise plans against strongholds, but only for a time.

Antiochus was known for handing out plunder lavishly to buy loyalty, something his ancestors had not done. But notice the phrase that keeps returning in this chapter: but only for a time. His plans have an expiry date set by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he shall stir up his power and his heart against the king of the south with a great army. And the king of the south shall wage war with an exceedingly great and mighty army, but he shall not stand, for plots shall be devised against him. Even those who eat his food shall break him. His army shall be swept away, and many shall fall down slain. And as for the two kings, their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for the end is yet to be at the time appointed. And he shall return to his land with great wealth, but his heart shall be set against the holy covenant. And he shall work his will and return to his own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he shall stir up his power and his heart against the king of the south with a great army. And the king of the south shall wage war with an exceedingly great and mighty army, but he shall not stand, for plots shall be devised against him.

Even those who eat his food shall break him. His army shall be swept away, and many shall fall down slain.

In 170-169 BC Antiochus invaded Egypt and defeated the young Ptolemy VI, who was betrayed by his own advisers, those who eat his food.

And as for the two kings, their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for the end is yet to be at the time appointed.

Antiochus and his defeated nephew sat down together, pretending friendship while each planned to deceive the other. They shall speak lies at the same table. What a picture of worldly politics. And what a contrast with the table of the Lord, where Christ gives himself in truth to his people. Yet even the lies of kings serve God's timetable: the end is yet to be at the time appointed.

And he shall return to his land with great wealth, but his heart shall be set against the holy covenant. And he shall work his will and return to his own land.

On his way home, in 169 BC, Antiochus entered Jerusalem and robbed the temple of its treasures. His heart was now set against the holy covenant, against God's people and their worship.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the time appointed he shall return and come into the south, but it shall not be this time as it was before. For ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant. He shall turn back and pay attention to those who forsake the holy covenant. Forces from him shall appear and profane the temple and fortress, and shall take away the regular burnt offering. And they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"At the time appointed he shall return and come into the south, but it shall not be this time as it was before.

For ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant. He shall turn back and pay attention to those who forsake the holy covenant.

In 168 BC Antiochus invaded Egypt again. But this time ships of Kittim arrived. "Kittim" originally meant Cyprus and came to be used of peoples from across the western sea. Here it means Rome. A Roman fleet brought an ambassador who ordered Antiochus to leave Egypt. When the king asked for time to think, the Roman drew a circle in the sand around him and told him to decide before he stepped out of it. Humiliated, Antiochus withdrew.

He took out his rage on the Jews. He found allies among those who forsake the holy covenant, Jews who wanted to abandon their faith and live like Greeks. Persecution from outside is often helped by compromise inside.

Forces from him shall appear and profane the temple and fortress, and shall take away the regular burnt offering. And they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.

In December 167 BC the daily sacrifices were stopped, and an altar to the Greek god Zeus was set up in God's temple, where unclean sacrifices were offered. This was the abomination that makes desolate, the outrage foretold in 8:11-13. Jesus later used the same phrase for a future desecration connected with the destruction of Jerusalem and the end (Matt 24:15). What Antiochus did became a pattern for later attacks on God's worship.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall seduce with flattery those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action. And the wise among the people shall make many understand, though for some days they shall stumble by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder. When they stumble, they shall receive a little help. And many shall join themselves to them with flattery, and some of the wise shall stumble, so that they may be refined, purified, and made white, until the time of the end, for it still awaits the appointed time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He shall seduce with flattery those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action.

This is the key verse of the chapter. Two kinds of people are named. Some violate the covenant, and the king wins them over with flattery, promises of position, safety and acceptance. Others are the people who know their God.

Notice what makes the difference. It is not how much they know about God, but whether they know their God. Knowing God personally, trusting him and loving him, is what enables believers to stand firm when the pressure comes. And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). And they take action. In 167 BC faithful Jews refused to sacrifice to idols, and a revolt began, led by a priestly family known as the Maccabees. Many refused to eat unclean food or abandon the law, even when it cost them their lives.

And the wise among the people shall make many understand, though for some days they shall stumble by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder.

The wise are those who understand God's word, and they teach others. Faithful teaching is one of the great weapons of God's people in persecution. But the wise also suffer: by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder. Hebrews probably has faithful people of this period in mind when it speaks of those who went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy (Heb 11:37-38).

When they stumble, they shall receive a little help. And many shall join themselves to them with flattery,

A little help probably refers to the military successes of the Maccabean revolt, which brought some relief. But it was only a little. The real deliverance of God's people would not come by the sword. And some who joined the cause did so insincerely, for their own advantage.

and some of the wise shall stumble, so that they may be refined, purified, and made white, until the time of the end, for it still awaits the appointed time.

Why does God allow even the wise to fall? So that they may be refined, purified, and made white. Suffering is God's fire for purifying his people, the way a metalworker heats silver to remove its impurities. He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver (Mal 3:3). Peter says the same to Christians: our trials come so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire—may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ (1 Pet 1:7). And even this suffering is limited: until the time of the end, the appointed time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–45 — The King Who Exalts Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods (v. 36). He honors no god but the god of fortresses and rewards his supporters (vv. 37-39). At the time of the end he sweeps through the countries and the glorious land and seizes Egypt's treasures (vv. 40-43). Alarmed by news from east and north, he goes out in fury and camps near the glorious holy mountain, Yet he shall come to his end, with none to help him (vv. 44-45).
verseByVerse.theology: The last great enemy of God will exalt himself above all, and he will come to his end.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods. He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done. He shall pay no attention to the gods of his fathers, or to the one beloved by women. He shall not pay attention to any other god, for he shall magnify himself above all. He shall honor the god of fortresses instead of these. A god whom his fathers did not know he shall honor with gold and silver, with precious stones and costly gifts. He shall deal with the strongest fortresses with the help of a foreign god. Those who acknowledge him he shall load with honor. He shall make them rulers over many and shall divide the land for a price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods. He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done.

With verse 36 we reach one of the most debated points in Daniel. Who is the king in verses 36-45?

Some believe the prophecy is still describing Antiochus IV. He did make great claims for himself and treated the gods of his fathers loosely. But the events of verses 40-45 do not match what we know of his last years. He did not conquer Egypt at the end of his life, and he did not die between the sea and Jerusalem. He died of illness in Persia.

Many others, including many in the Reformed tradition and most dispensational interpreters, believe that at this point the prophecy looks beyond Antiochus to the final enemy of God at the end of history, the little horn of chapter 7 and the man of lawlessness described by Paul. Antiochus was a preview of him, a small-scale picture of the final great rebellion. Paul seems to echo this very verse when he writes that the man of lawlessness exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship... proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thess 2:4). The phrase At the time of the end in verse 40 also points in this direction. These notes follow this second view, while recognizing that the line between Antiochus and the final enemy is not sharply drawn. The prophecy moves from the near horizon to the far one, the way a traveler sees nearby hills and distant mountains as one skyline.

Either way, the chief mark of this king is pride. He shall do as he wills. He exalts himself above every god. He speaks astonishing things against the God of gods. But he, too, is on a leash: He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done. God has decreed the limit.

He shall pay no attention to the gods of his fathers, or to the one beloved by women. He shall not pay attention to any other god, for he shall magnify himself above all.

He has no loyalty to any religion, only to himself. The one beloved by women is obscure. It may refer to a god especially popular with women in the ancient world, or to the natural desire for love and family, which this king despises. The main point is clear: he shall magnify himself above all.

He shall honor the god of fortresses instead of these. A god whom his fathers did not know he shall honor with gold and silver, with precious stones and costly gifts.

He shall deal with the strongest fortresses with the help of a foreign god. Those who acknowledge him he shall load with honor. He shall make them rulers over many and shall divide the land for a price.

The only god he truly worships is the god of fortresses: military power. Whatever he says he believes, his real trust is in force. And he buys loyalty by rewarding those who support him. It is a portrait of every godless tyrant, and of the final one.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the time of the end, the king of the south shall attack him, but the king of the north shall rush upon him like a whirlwind, with chariots and horsemen, and with many ships. And he shall come into countries and shall overflow and pass through. He shall come into the glorious land. And tens of thousands shall fall, but these shall be delivered out of his hand: Edom and Moab and the main part of the Ammonites. He shall stretch out his hand against the countries, and the land of Egypt shall not escape. He shall become ruler of the treasures of gold and of silver, and all the precious things of Egypt, and the Libyans and the Cushites shall follow in his train. But news from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and devote many to destruction. And he shall pitch his palatial tents between the sea and the glorious holy mountain. Yet he shall come to his end, with none to help him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"At the time of the end, the king of the south shall attack him, but the king of the north shall rush upon him like a whirlwind, with chariots and horsemen, and with many ships. And he shall come into countries and shall overflow and pass through.

At the time of the end, the conflicts of the past are repeated on a larger scale. (The ESV notes that attack is literally "thrust at".) The last enemy sweeps through the world like a whirlwind.

He shall come into the glorious land. And tens of thousands shall fall, but these shall be delivered out of his hand: Edom and Moab and the main part of the Ammonites.

He shall stretch out his hand against the countries, and the land of Egypt shall not escape.

He shall become ruler of the treasures of gold and of silver, and all the precious things of Egypt, and the Libyans and the Cushites shall follow in his train.

He enters the glorious land, the land of God's people, and conquers Egypt and its neighbors. Edom, Moab and Ammon, Israel's ancient enemies, escape him, perhaps because they side with him. Libya and Cush (the lands to the west and south of Egypt) follow him. The names are those of Daniel's world, but the picture is of a ruler who seems to hold all the wealth and power of the earth.

But news from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and devote many to destruction.

And he shall pitch his palatial tents between the sea and the glorious holy mountain. Yet he shall come to his end, with none to help him.

Then comes a sudden alarm. The picture recalls how God dealt with the Assyrian king Sennacherib long before: he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land (Isa 37:7). The greatest ruler on earth can be shaken by a report. The conqueror turns in fury, and he sets up his royal camp between the sea and the glorious holy mountain, close to Jerusalem, where God's name dwells. It looks as though he is about to make his final attack on God's people.

And then, in a single sentence, it is over. Yet he shall come to his end, with none to help him. No battle is described. No army saves him. The one who helped his supporters (v. 39) has no one to help him. Paul says of the final enemy that the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming (2 Thess 2:8).

That is the message of this long, difficult chapter. Kings plot, marry, betray, invade and plunder. Empires rise and fall. God's people suffer in the middle of it all. But every event was known to God before it happened, every enemy is given only a time, and the last and greatest enemy will come to his end. The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples. The counsel of the LORD stands forever (Ps 33:10-11). Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Cor 15:25). Until then, the calling of God's people is the calling of verse 32: to know our God, to stand firm and to act.

11.title: The People Who Know Their God
11.overview:
The messenger, who strengthened Michael in the first year of Darius, reveals the truth: three more kings will arise in Persia, and a fourth, far richer, will stir up all against Greece. A mighty king will then rule with great dominion, but his kingdom will be broken and divided toward the four winds, not to his descendants (vv. 1-4).

The king of the south and the king of the north make and break a marriage alliance, invade each other's lands, carry off gods and treasures, and raise great armies. The king of the north takes a fortified city, stands in the glorious land, gives a daughter in marriage without gain, turns to the coastlands where a commander ends his insolence, and falls. His successor sends an exactor of tribute and is soon broken (vv. 5-20).

A contemptible person obtains the kingdom by flatteries, sweeps away armies and the prince of the covenant, acts deceitfully, invades the south and sits at one table with its king speaking lies. With his heart set against the holy covenant, he returns; opposed by ships of Kittim, he turns in rage against the covenant, profanes the temple, removes the regular burnt offering and sets up the abomination that makes desolate. He seduces covenant-breakers with flattery, but the people who know their God stand firm and act. The wise teach many and suffer by sword, flame, captivity and plunder, and some stumble so that they may be refined until the time of the end (vv. 21-35).

The king does as he wills, exalts himself above every god, speaks astonishing things against the God of gods and honors the god of fortresses, rewarding those who acknowledge him. At the time of the end he sweeps through countries, enters the glorious land, conquers Egypt and takes its treasures. Alarmed by news from the east and north, he goes out in fury and pitches his tents between the sea and the glorious holy mountain, yet he comes to his end with none to help him (vv. 36-45).
11.theology:
God knows the whole course of history in detail before it happens, and the plans of kings serve his purpose (vv. 2-35; Prov 19:21; Ps 33:10-11).

Human alliances, marriages and schemes cannot secure lasting peace or power (vv. 6, 17, 27).

God sees the proud as contemptible, whatever they call themselves (v. 21).

Persecution of God's people is aided by compromise within, but those who know their God stand firm and act (vv. 30, 32; John 17:3).

Faithful teachers strengthen God's people, and God uses suffering to refine and purify them for a limited, appointed time (vv. 33-35; Mal 3:3; 1 Pet 1:6-7; Heb 11:36-38).

The final enemy of God will exalt himself above every god, but he will come to his end, destroyed by the Lord Jesus at his coming (vv. 36-45; 2 Thess 2:4, 8; 1 Cor 15:25).
11.examples:
A Persian king rich enough to invade Greece.

A royal marriage meant to bring peace that ends in murder.

A small land caught between two empires.

A self-styled god whom God calls contemptible.

Two kings telling lies at the same table.

A circle drawn in the sand around a humiliated king.

An idol's altar in God's temple.

Ordinary believers who know their God and will not bow.

And there shall be a time of trouble, such as never has been since there was a nation till that time. But at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book.<sup>2</sup>And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.<sup>3</sup>And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.<sup>4</sup>But you, Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end. Then I said, "O my lord, what shall be the outcome of these things?"<sup>9</sup>He said, "Go your way, Daniel, for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end.<sup>10</sup>Many shall purify themselves and make themselves white and be refined, but the wicked shall act wickedly.
