And you shall rest and shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At that time shall arise Michael, the great prince who has charge of your people. There will be a time of trouble, such as never has been, but your people shall be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book (v. 1). And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt (v. 2). The wise will shine like the sky, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars forever (v. 3). Daniel is to seal the book until the time of the end (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: History ends not in the grave but in resurrection, judgment and glory for those whose names are written in God's book.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time shall arise Michael, the great prince who has charge of your people. And there shall be a time of trouble, such as never has been since there was a nation till that time. But at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"At that time shall arise Michael, the great prince who has charge of your people. And there shall be a time of trouble, such as never has been since there was a nation till that time. But at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book.

The chapter division here is unfortunate. This verse continues straight on from the end of chapter 11. At that time means the time when the final enemy of God makes his last attack, and he shall come to his end (11:45). The long vision that began in chapter 10 now reaches its climax.

First, Michael arises. We met him in 10:13, 21 as the great angel who fights for Daniel's people. At the decisive moment, heaven acts on their behalf.

Second, there shall be a time of trouble, such as never has been. The final days will bring suffering greater than any before. Jesus took up these very words when he spoke of the end: For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be (Matt 24:21). Christians understand this in different ways. Some, including dispensationalists, believe it describes a specific future period of great tribulation just before Christ returns. Many others, including many Reformed interpreters, believe the whole age between Christ's first and second comings is marked by tribulation for the church, rising to a final, terrible intensity before the end. Both agree that believers should not be surprised by suffering, and that it will not have the last word.

Third, and most important, your people shall be delivered. And the verse tells us exactly who: everyone whose name shall be found written in the book. This is God's book of life, the register of those who belong to him. Moses spoke of it (Exod 32:32). Jesus told his disciples, rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Revelation calls it the book of life of the Lamb who was slain (Rev 13:8), and the risen Christ promises the one who conquers, I will never blot his name out of the book of life (Rev 3:5).

This is the deepest comfort in the whole book of Daniel. When the worst comes, God's people will not be kept safe by their own strength, nationality or cleverness. They will be kept because God has written their names in his book, and he does not lose what is his. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28).

verseByVerse.quote: And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

This is one of the clearest promises of the resurrection of the body in the whole Old Testament. Death is described as sleep in the dust of the earth. Since the fall, God's sentence on humanity has been you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). But the dust is not the end. Those who sleep there shall awake.

Calling death "sleep" does not mean the dead are unconscious or that death is unreal. It means that death is not permanent. Sleep is followed by waking. That is why Paul could say to grieving Christians, we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13).

The resurrection will divide humanity into two destinies. Some to everlasting life. And some to shame and everlasting contempt. The same word, everlasting, describes both. Jesus said the same: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28-29). And he said, these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matt 25:46).

Why does the verse say many rather than all? Some believe many here means the great multitude of the dead, that is, everyone, as Jesus' words suggest. Others think the verse focuses on the people of Daniel's own story, the faithful and the apostate of the final conflict. Either way, the rest of Scripture is clear that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust (Acts 24:15).

This verse changes everything about how we read the rest of Daniel. Many faithful people in this book were not rescued from death. The wise stumble by sword and flame (11:33). If this life were all, the persecutors would have won. But this verse shows that the martyrs will awake to everlasting life, and their persecutors to everlasting shame. And we know how this hope is secured. Jesus Christ has already risen from the dust. I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live (John 11:25).

verseByVerse.quote: And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever. But you, Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end. Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall increase."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.

Those who are wise are the faithful teachers of 11:33, who make many understand even when it costs them their lives. On earth they were despised and killed. In the resurrection they will shine. The ESV notes that the sky above is literally "the expanse", the same word used in Genesis 1:6-8 for the sky God made on the second day of creation. Their glory will be as wide and bright as the heavens.

Jesus used the same picture: Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt 13:43).

Notice who shines brightest: those who turn many to righteousness. They are not the famous or powerful of this world. They are the people who taught others the truth and led them to God. A Sunday school teacher, a parent who prays with her children, a faithful pastor in a small church, a believer who quietly shares Christ with a friend at work: these are the ones who will shine like the stars forever and ever. Even now, Paul says, believers shine as lights in the world (Phil 2:15). One day the light will be complete.

But you, Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end. Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall increase."

Daniel is told to seal the book. As in 8:26, this means to preserve it securely, not to hide it. It is like a legal document, sealed and kept safe until the time it is needed. Those who live through the events it describes will open it and understand.

Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall increase. This phrase is often quoted as a prediction of modern travel and scientific progress. That is almost certainly not what it means. The prophet Amos used the same picture of people who shall run to and fro, to seek the word of the LORD, but they shall not find it (Amos 8:12). Here the idea seems to be that many will search anxiously for understanding in troubled times, and that, as history unfolds, knowledge of the meaning of Daniel's prophecy will grow. The sealed book will become clearer as its words come true.

That has proved true. Daniel did not understand much of what he saw (v. 8). The Jews who suffered under Antiochus understood more. And we, who live after the coming of Christ, can see even further. In the last book of the Bible, John is told the opposite of what Daniel was told: Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near (Rev 22:10). With the coming of Jesus, the end has drawn near.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two figures stand on the riverbanks, and one asks the man clothed in linen, How long shall it be till the end of these wonders? He swears by the one who lives forever: a time, times, and half a time, until the shattering of the power of the holy people is complete (vv. 5-7). Daniel does not understand and is told, Go your way, Daniel; many will be purified, the wicked will act wickedly, and the wise will understand (vv. 8-10). There will be 1,290 days, and Blessed is he who waits and arrives at the 1,335 days (vv. 11-12). But go your way till the end. And you shall rest and shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people are not given every date, but they are given a promise, and they wait, endure and rest in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I, Daniel, looked, and behold, two others stood, one on this bank of the stream and one on that bank of the stream. And someone said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream, "How long shall it be till the end of these wonders?" And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream; he raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven and swore by him who lives forever that it would be for a time, times, and half a time, and that when the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end all these things would be finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I, Daniel, looked, and behold, two others stood, one on this bank of the stream and one on that bank of the stream.

The vision returns to the scene by the river where it began (10:4). Two more heavenly figures appear, one on each bank. In the Law of Moses, two witnesses were needed to confirm a matter (Deut 19:15). Perhaps these two stand as witnesses to the oath that is about to be sworn.

And someone said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream, "How long shall it be till the end of these wonders?"

The man clothed in linen of 10:5 stands above the waters. (The ESV notes this may mean he was "upstream".) One of the witnesses asks the question every suffering believer asks: How long? How long until these terrible and wonderful things are finished?

And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream; he raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven and swore by him who lives forever that it would be for a time, times, and half a time, and that when the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end all these things would be finished.

The answer is given with a solemn oath. Normally a person raised one hand to swear an oath. This figure raises both hands toward heaven and swears by him who lives forever. Nothing could be more certain. Revelation echoes this scene, when a mighty angel raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever that there would be no more delay (Rev 10:5-6).

The length is a time, times, and half a time, the same limited period we saw in 7:25. (For the two main ways Christians understand it, see the note there.) It is a real period of suffering, but it is measured, and it is broken off before it can become complete.

And the end will come when the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end. That is a startling statement. The end does not come when God's people are strongest. It comes when their power has been completely broken. God often waits until his people have nothing left, so that the victory is plainly his. My power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9). The same was true at the cross. When Jesus hung dead and his followers were scattered, the power of God's holy people seemed utterly shattered. Three days later, death itself was defeated.

verseByVerse.quote: I heard, but I did not understand. Then I said, "O my lord, what shall be the outcome of these things?" He said, "Go your way, Daniel, for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end. Many shall purify themselves and make themselves white and be refined, but the wicked shall act wickedly. And none of the wicked shall understand, but those who are wise shall understand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I heard, but I did not understand. Then I said, "O my lord, what shall be the outcome of these things?"

How honest this is. After a lifetime of interpreting dreams and receiving visions, Daniel admits: I heard, but I did not understand. The greatest prophet of the exile did not have every answer about the future. That should humble anyone who claims to have worked out every detail of biblical prophecy. If Daniel did not understand, we should hold our own theories with humility.

He said, "Go your way, Daniel, for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end.

Go your way, Daniel. This is not a rebuke. It is a gentle release. Daniel does not need to understand everything. He needs to trust God and keep living faithfully. Jesus said something similar to his disciples when they asked about the timing of the kingdom: It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority (Acts 1:7). God has not given us a timetable to calculate. He has given us a promise to live by.

Many shall purify themselves and make themselves white and be refined, but the wicked shall act wickedly. And none of the wicked shall understand, but those who are wise shall understand.

The coming troubles will have two opposite effects. Some will be purified by them, made white and refined like metal in the fire (11:35). Others will simply go on doing evil. The same suffering that sanctifies one person hardens another. Revelation says the same about the last days: Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy (Rev 22:11).

And those who are wise shall understand. Understanding God's purposes is not a matter of intelligence but of faith. The wicked cannot understand because they will not submit to God. The wise understand because they fear him. The revelation of Jesus Christ, when it comes, will make everything clear to those who have waited for him (1 Pet 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And from the time that the regular burnt offering is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate is set up, there shall be 1,290 days. Blessed is he who waits and arrives at the 1,335 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And from the time that the regular burnt offering is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate is set up, there shall be 1,290 days.

Blessed is he who waits and arrives at the 1,335 days.

These two numbers are among the most puzzling in Daniel, and it is best to be honest: no one can be certain what they mean. Both numbers are a little longer than three and a half years (about 1,260 days, as in Rev 11:3). The first adds thirty days, and the second adds another forty-five.

Christians have understood them in several ways. Some apply them to the persecution under Antiochus IV, counting from the desecration of the temple to the end of that crisis. Some, especially dispensationalists, see them as extra periods after a future seven-year tribulation, perhaps for judgment and the setting up of Christ's kingdom. Others take the numbers symbolically, as a way of saying that the time of trouble may last a little longer than God's people expect, and they must keep waiting even when the end seems overdue.

Whatever the exact meaning, the verse puts its emphasis on one word: Blessed. Blessed is he who waits and arrives. The blessing does not go to the person who calculates the date. It goes to the person who waits faithfully and endures to the end. Jesus said, the one who endures to the end will be saved (Matt 24:13), and concerning that day and hour no one knows (Matt 24:36). The call of prophecy is not to predict but to persevere.

verseByVerse.quote: But go your way till the end. And you shall rest and shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But go your way till the end. And you shall rest and shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days."

The book of Daniel ends with a personal word to an old man. Daniel had been carried away from home as a boy. He had served four kings and two empires. He had faced lions, seen visions that made him sick and prayed for a city he would never see again. Now he is told three things.

Go your way till the end. Keep living faithfully for the time you have left. Daniel would not see the fulfilment of his visions. Like all the faithful of the Old Testament, he would die not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb 11:13).

And you shall rest. Daniel would die. But for the believer, death is rest from labor. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on... that they may rest from their labors (Rev 14:13).

And shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days. Daniel will rise again. He was one of those who sleep in the dust, and he will awake. And he will stand in his allotted place. When Israel entered the promised land, each family received its inheritance by lot (Josh 14:2). Daniel had lost his home in Judah. But God had kept an inheritance for him that no empire could take. The psalmist said, The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot (Ps 16:5).

That promise belongs to every believer in Christ. We have been born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Pet 1:3-4). Jesus said, I go to prepare a place for you (John 14:2).

So the book that began with the fall of Jerusalem and a teenager carried off to Babylon ends with an old man told to rest in hope of the resurrection. In between, kings raged, empires rose and fell, and beasts made war on the saints. But the Most High ruled over all of it. The stone cut without hands has struck the image. The Son of Man has received the kingdom. The Anointed One has been cut off for our sins and raised to life. And one day all who sleep in the dust will hear his voice. Until then, the word to Daniel is the word to every Christian: go your way, be faithful, and wait for him. The Lord Jesus says, Surely I am coming soon, and his church answers, Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! (Rev 22:20).

12.title: Those Who Sleep in the Dust Shall Awake
12.overview:
At that time Michael, the great prince who has charge of Daniel's people, will arise. There will be a time of trouble unlike any since nations began, but Daniel's people will be delivered, everyone whose name is written in the book. Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt. The wise will shine like the sky, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars forever. Daniel is to seal the book until the time of the end, when many will run to and fro and knowledge will increase (vv. 1-4).

Two others stand on the banks of the stream, and one asks the man clothed in linen how long it will be until the end of these wonders. Raising both hands to heaven, he swears by him who lives forever that it will be for a time, times and half a time, and that all will be finished when the shattering of the power of the holy people ends (vv. 5-7).

Daniel hears but does not understand, and asks the outcome. He is told to go his way, for the words are sealed until the end; many will be purified and refined, the wicked will act wickedly, and only the wise will understand. From the removal of the regular burnt offering and the setting up of the abomination there will be 1,290 days; blessed is the one who waits and reaches the 1,335 days. Daniel is to go his way till the end; he will rest and will stand in his allotted place at the end of the days (vv. 8-13).
12.theology:
God delivers all whose names are written in his book, even through the greatest tribulation (v. 1; Matt 24:21; Luke 10:20; Rev 3:5; 13:8; John 10:28).

The dead will be raised bodily, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame, a hope secured by the resurrection of Jesus Christ (v. 2; John 5:28-29; 11:25; Matt 25:46; Acts 24:15; 1 Thess 4:13-14).

Those who are wise and turn many to righteousness will shine forever (v. 3; Matt 13:43; Phil 2:15).

God's word about the future is certain, sworn by him who lives forever, and his people's suffering is limited and ends when their own power is spent (vv. 6-7; Rev 10:5-6; 2 Cor 12:9).

Even prophets do not understand everything; God's people are called not to calculate dates but to wait, endure and be refined (vv. 8-12; Acts 1:7; Matt 24:13, 36; Rev 22:11).

Believers rest in death and will rise to receive the inheritance God has kept for them (v. 13; Heb 11:13; Rev 14:13; Ps 16:5-6; 1 Pet 1:3-4; John 14:2-3).
12.examples:
A book with the names of God's people written in it.

Graves described as beds from which the sleepers will wake.

A Sunday school teacher who will shine like a star.

An oath sworn with both hands raised to heaven.

A great prophet who says, "I did not understand."

A blessing promised not to the one who calculates, but to the one who waits.

An old exile told to rest, and promised a place of his own.
